SAN ANTONIO, Tex, June Is
U.N.SO.-With at least nine per
sons dead, scores missing, and
many highway and railway bridges
washed out, southwest Texas to-
day battled new flood menaces as
torrential rains sent streams flood
ing out of their banks.


Raging waters of the Colorado
River swept into Austin, the State
capital, this morning, put the city
water and municipal light plant
out of commission and flooded
lowlands of the city.


The known death toll included
five at Del Rio, three at Karnes
City, and one at Victoria. Many
persons were missing over a wide
area.


The Nueces River spread out
over a four-mile area at Uvalde,
with water several inches deep in
the business district. The Nueces
was reported falling, but a new
threat came from Leona Greek,
which runs directly through the
town. Families were moved to
higher ground. Two highway
bridges and railway bridge were
out.

BERLIN, November 2.-Belief that
Reichsfuehrer Hitler will end the life
of the Steel Helmet veterans organi-
zation before November 9 was ex-
pressed tonight by spokesmen of the
proud society.


They said the initiative was now
up to Hitler, who would have Diff
Guilty making a decision. But they
asserted they hoped the organization
would break up "as soon as possible
| because Of the many misunderstand-
ings and difficulties due to the knowl-
edge that the organization is on the
way out"


They had predicted previously that
the result Of many conferences be.
tween Hitler and Franz Seldte, labor
minister and Stahlhelm chief, would
be decision to "disband voluntarily"
The ex-soldiers' association had played
a big part in affairs of Germany until
Nazidom felt it threatened the Hit
lerite totalitarian ideal.


Proud of Traditions.


The Steel Helmets have declared
themselves too proud of their tradi-
tions and deeds to take the face-sav-
ing way out offered by the Nazis-that
of merging with other and less prom
inent veterans groups.


The end of the Stahlhelm will mark
another Hitlerite step toward abolish
ing all organizations not 100 per cent
Nazi-regardless Of past favors and
promises.


The Steel Helmets dominated the
national scene until several months
ago. when Hitler's subleaders subjected
the veterans unit to harrying indig-
mites. Their offenses, in NaA eyes,
seemed to consist of conservatism, re-
actionism and something less than
complete Nazi-ism. They we're called
state enemies" in the late-Summer
drive against Jewry. political Catholi-
cism and other "dissidents."


Clashes Frequent.


Before Hitler assumed power, the
Steel Helmets and the Storm Troops
often clashed. But on January 20,
1888, when it was rumoSed that Gen.
Won Schleicher was mobilizing the
Potsdam garrison to erect a military
dictatorship, Seldte agreed to join his
forces with Hitier's "to save the coun-
try"


Since then. however, the Brown
Shirts and the Gray Shirts have had
frequent differences. In its heyday
the Stahlhelm numbered about 1,500,-
600 men. Since July, 1885, however.
its numbers have rapidly fallen.

WE SAID the other day that fash
w ion is kind to all types this year.
True. But she still favors the slen-
der. What world of lovely things to
choose from this year. What styles.
What colors What fabrics.


In sports wear, for instance. The
swagger, cleverly cut, casual coats
are fine for the thin types. The pain
fully thin, however. better note right
here that they had better add few
pounds before attempting the swag-
gers, lest they hang and thereby call
attention to the scarecrow frame be-
meath.


The sports suits that scramble their
colors are fine. The plaids and high
colors particularly for they give the
slender figure broader look.


The draped effects for evening are
again intended for the slender. The
front fullness. the shorter skirts, the
draped neckerchiefs, the fluffy furs.
the military vogue with its braid
trappings, frog trimmings. the cape
lets of fur on cloth dresses-what a
world of beauty and variety-all in
tended for the slender.


Just as the stout type should be
careful to choose vertical. up and
down or v lines in her clothes and
accessories, so the thin type should
stick to horizontal lines. lines that
carry the eye across and thus give
an illusion of breadth. Full sleeves
are good for this reason. Whether
the fullness is concentrated at the
shoulder, elbow or wrist makes little
diference-the eye is carried across
in every one of these fashions. Wide
bracelets at the wrist are charming
and particularly becoming to slender
wrists. The forentine jewelry beads
and gold circles at the throat are
very f1attering and short choker ef-
fects are better for the thin throat
than the longer beads. A word about
this type of jewelry, though; if you
are very thin don't wear the very
massive jewelry. 1t will seem too
overpowering.


The frilly, lacy collars are decidedly
feminine and altogether flattering to
the thin type, particularly the round,
short collars which make the face
and neck seem rounder.


High colors belong to the thin type,
and this year more than any other
fashion offers such a riot of gorgeous
high shades and such a scramble of
colors that there is little excuse for
remaining in a rut Of drabness. Step
out and dare to be different.

FORT SMITH, Ark, December 81


P).-In the Ozarks they're pre-
pairing once more for homemade
Christmas.


The hillfolk have come a long way
from the hardships and customs of
their foraebears, but they still have
little need for "store-bought" gifts,
fashioning their own with hands
adept at woodworking and quilting.


This country of hollows and hog
backs is true setting for the most
important event of the year. Cedars,
pines and mistletoe abound on every
hand. Holly may be found in spots.
One large source of spending money
to the natives is the selling Of Christ
mas trees.


Woven and knitted articles make up
the women's contributions to the holi-
day, besides their cooking. The men
folk fashion benches, chairs, tables
and novelties.

PLANT hunters, those unsung heroes


who scour the far places of the
earth in their search for forms of
plant life usable in the United States
for crossing with certain American
plants to secure better product, are
concentrating on the drought-re-
sistant plants at present.


Scientists of the Department of Ag-
riculture have recently sent back seeds
of 1900 different plants from Turke-
stan which have pronounced drought
resistant characteristics. Other
seeds have arrived from Mongolia
and Manchuria, while still others are
awaited from the Cobb Desert.


China, with her denuded hills alter
mating between flobd and drought, has
been forced, through grim necessity,
to concentrate on those forms of plant
life which can resist drought, and it
is these plants which are being
brought here for experimentation and
development in some of the dry sec
tions of the United States.

HOLLYWOOD, Nov. 2.-"1t

the field to blast the statement to
bits.


With the radio, the growing i'm

motion picture pubIc's change Of
heart in welcoming able stage tai
ent over mere personality, stars
are coming to the American screen
practically ready.made.


Both Burns and Allen and Jack
Benny had their vast radio pub
lie ready and waiting to put their
money down at the box office
when they made their film debutS.
Joe Penner's following flocked to

on the screen. The same holds
true with the songsters who were.

headlinerS, such as Lilly Pons,
Grace Moore, Nelson Eddy, Gladys

Paley.

Sir Ronald Lindsay, the British

The British envoy has in

mittee to make public the cor.
respondence between the British

Guaranty Trust Company and

SubpOenaS Planned


Britain took this step following
word that the Senate Munitions

Morgan companies to produce
correspondence dealing with pur-
chaSes of ammunition for Great
Britain during the war.


Sir Dnno1l inIcou in tolyiI9o
the matter up with the State De
partment, gave the impression
that the British government was
not moved to object by any fear
Of what the correspondence might
reveal but rather because of the
principle involved.


The British government, Sir
Ronald made it plain, feels that
its relations with its fiscal agents
in foreign countries are private
matters which should not be
made public by any foreign parlia-
ment without its consent.


Opposes Publicity


Sir Ronald left the impression
that the British government would
have no objection to the Senate
Munitions Committee seeing the
correspondence providing it did
not make it public.


The British governments views
have been transmitted by the
State Department to the Senate
Munitions Committee, but the de-
partment has not otherwise taken
any stand in the matter.


Brita1n's concern led to the be-

banking houses might reveal some
views Of the British government

ton in other countries that might
embarrass London at the present
time.

By the Associated Press.


SAARBRUECKEN, Saar Basin Ter
ritory, January "a battle between
Nazis and anti-Nazis broke out at
noon today In Waterloo sGreet, but was
quickly suppressed by overwhelming
forces of police and the landjaeger
(gendarmes).


The section where the turmoil
reigned is one of the city's choicer
residence districts, and the Nazi Ger
man Front headquarters are located
on Waterloo street.


1t was Waterloo for both sides, for
Maj. Hennessey, chief of the Saar
civil police, personally led the forces
Of law and order into the fray and
squelched the combat before 1t could
develop beyond the fisticuff, club and
kicking stage.


Propaganda Papers Scattered.


The riot started when a detachment
of adherents to the proposal that the
Saar Basin Territory should stay I'M
der the League of Nations, raided
Waterloo street, scattering propaganda
newspapers on the sidewalks and in
the front yards of homes.


Several hundred Nazis Immediately
appeared and battle royal began.


Heads popped out of windows all
along the street. Most of the heads
emitted cheers for the Nazi side.


In a few minutes police lorries
roared into the thick of the fighting
and other police surrounded the battle
area. They took many names but, ac-
cording to Maj. HennesSey, made no
arrests.


Both sides claimed they had suf-
fered wounded but no one was sent
to hospital.


German Border Watched.


Police are being concentrated along
the German border, it was disclosed
today, in final preparation for the
Saar plebiscite Sunday.


The landjaeger (Gendarmes), de-
spite the protests Of NaZis, have been
shifted by the Governing Commits
sion from the French to the Ger
man side Of the territory, leaving the
French border protected only by
municipal policemen and 100 Italian
troops.


Nazis are furious over the obvious
intimation that, If trouble comes CT
the momentous Sunday, it will come
from Germany. They protested,
charging the landjaeger had been
withdrawn principally in the Warfdt
district, where it has been predicted
most of the votes will favor a union
with France.


Spies Swarm Territory.


Spies swarm throughout the terri
tory. Tales of espionage and cCun-
ter espionage are recounted daily


Documents from one side or the
other disappear almost daily, some-
times, it is said, from locked safes.
A museum" composed largely Of
such documents, will be opened to-
night by Nazis at Kaiserslautern,
Germany, 10 miles from the Saar
frontier.


Preliminary voting ends today when
circulating voting bureau finishes
its rounds Of hospitals and prisons.


Those Arrested May Vote.


Most of the civil employees eligible
to vote Monday and Tuesday decided
to wait until Sunday to cast their
ballots. The commission has ruled
that all persons arrested between now
and Sunday will be permitted to 60
to the polls accompanied by guard.


Communists, who favor remaining
under the League of Nations, may
not win against Nazis. eager to af-
filiate with the Germany of adolf
Hitler, but early today they still had
the upper hand of the Nazi municipal
government here, which seeks to oust
them from their headquarters.


The city government recently bought
the building containing the head
quarters, but the Communists ignored
an eviction notice. Throughout last
night they defied police to oust them.

After joining the Daughters Of

ganizing branches. Her ardor cooled,

The women withdrew, met in an

convention, for men and women, and
were successful in getting good
membership in the State. Horace
Greely of the New York Tribune ad-
vised them as to the proper procedure.
Elizabeth Cady Stanton was elected
president and Susan B. Anthony Sec
retary. The public seemed to be as
much opposed as the Sons of Temper
ance to having the women speak in
public, but the members persevered

sorts of attacks and vile hootings of

decided that in order to obtain any

She Joined the Woman's Rights
Society and became very active, bear

and meeting places and standing for

ences tried by abuse to scare the
speakers and prevent their being
heard. Miss Anthony canvassed each

reforms. She was never actually
mobbed, but no woman was ever nearer

For the eleventh consecutive year
Washingtonians are enjoying reduc-
ton in their rates for electricity.
While the reduction this year is not
so great, the significant point is that
the working agreement between the
electric light company and the Public
Utilities Commission continues to
function, and the reduction. agreed
upon as fair in relation to the COM
pany's earnings, is made without re-
sort to litigation or ill-feeling between
the company and the consumers.


The first power rate reduction was
ordered by the then newly created
Public Utilities Commission In 1917,
when the rate for domestic consump-
ton was ten cents for the first 100
kilowatts. That order and succeeding
orders of the commission were en-
Joined until the consent decree OF
1924, which gave the city It's first rate
reduction IN 1925. The order which
became effective last midnight reduces
domestic rates to 3.9 cents for the
first fifty kilowatts and to 81 cents
for the second fifty, with further re-
ductions for higher consumption.


1t is little wonder that the wash
ington plan" for rate reduction is at
tracing such an increasing amount Of
attention from other cities where
high rates are adding force to the
arguments tor public ownership and
operation of municipal plants. If
other power companies were willing to
apply the Washington plan they
might save themselves the battle for
their continued existence which lies
ahead.

FALLS CHURCH, Va, Aug. 81.
Theories to explain the Staying Of
Truman Brush, 76-year-old recluse
whose battered body was found in
the woods near his tumbling log
cabin last Friday, were reduced
today to one.


Several officers working on the
case, after sitting evidence and
questioning neighbors and friends
Of the aged victim, whose head
was crushed with two heavy rocks,
concluded that the once prosper
Gus farmer was killed by someone
who knew his habits and the Sc
cluded path he used to visit his
friend, Hugh Hummer, the neigh
Dor who discovered his body.


Story Reconstructed


The tragic story was recon
Structed as follows:


Shortly after 3 p. m. Friday Mr..
Brush walked over to the house
Of ]. I. Vandermark, who lives on
the nearest travelled road, and
waited for the bread truck that
serves that road to come through.
Mr., Vandermark said it was be-
tween 3 and 4 o'clock when Mr..
Brush bought a loaf Of bread and
left for his bleak quarters several
hundred feet away.


Returning to his quarters, the
aged man placed his loaf Of bread
in a basket that hangs from the
wall, came out again, locked his
door and started down the hidden
path toward Mr.. Hummer'S house.
The day before, according to Mr..
Hummer, Mr.: Brush had asked
him to bring him some pills from
the drug store here and said he
would call for them Friday.


Time Was Short


Less than 100 yards from his
house, but in the thickets that
surround his dwelling, the thrifty
old farmer was attacked and
beaten to death. The slayer is
believed to have made a hurried
search Of the farmers house and
then fled.


Two factors that point out that
the murderer had little time to
ranSack the house are that the
body was still warm and limp
when authorities reached the
scene; and that the loaf of bread
had been placed in its usual, but
odd, place, and the door locked,
which indicated that the house
had been ransacked after the
murder.


Another fact that indicates the
house was hurriedly searched is
that yesterday officers found
three separate containers in which
the recluSe had hid his money
a sum described as "large," but
less than $1,000-overlooked by
the earlier Searcher.

The infant mortality rate in Wash
ington last week was the second
highest of cities along the Eastern
seaboard, and only 10 of all the cities

Only five cities had a higher in

The rate of death among the chill

geonS, governments and citizens have

Improved and expanded hospital

for expectant mothers are two of the
most needed methods of lessening the
percentage of babies who die in their
first year, the most crucial year of
their existence.


Clinic Wages Campaign.


In Washington, the Infant Clinic
of Columbia Hospital for Women is
waging more strongly than any other
institution a campaign aimed at max
ing available to every mother or ex-
pectant mother in the city informa-
ton and care that will insure a
stronger, healthier baby, one more
likely to survive the first few months
Of its harsh existence.


Last year patients made 1906
visits to the clinic. They were given
physical examinations. They were
taught the responsibilities, duties and
general physiological problems at
tendant upon motherhood.


The poorest were provided with
transportation to and from the clinic.
Some were given layettes if their
finances prevented their purchasing
them. They were provided with maga-

hours.


The social service department of
the clinic, which includes one full
time worker and % part-time volun-
teer workers, paid 2,213 calls to the
homes of patients registered to see
that the lessons taught at the clinic
we're followed religiously.


The effect of this endeavor is to
flt the mother properly for the birth

the baby during its tender initiation
into the ways of its separate existence.
The most marked result is an instant
decrease in the infant mortality and
the rate of stillbirth among the group
so taught and supervised.


The clinic is run by Miss Linda
Woods under the direction of the
Women's Board of Columbia Hospital,

whom the clinics recent amazing
progress is due. Its money comes
from the Community Chest, the
Thrift Shop, assessments against
members of the board and from the
small fees asked, when payable, from
the patients who come to the clinic.


Facilities Increased.


The clinic in 1920 was a two-room
establishment under one worker. To-
day it has eight rooms, fitted with
baby scales, baby baskets, beds, clos
cts, medical apparatus and other
equipment necessary to perform Its
function.

far more than merely provide for
bare care and instruction of the

magazines for teaching and enter

window boxes filled with flowers each

inspect Norwegian country life at
first hand.

~ France is moving slowly but

mere stepping stones leading toward
a grand finale. The sporadic riots,
demonstrations and protests now go
ing on against high prices, wage and
pension cuts, etc, are slight symp-
toms of a widespread and growing
unrest.


In reality the three-month in

ment granted Premier Laval author

when the Chamber meets again-is
but an armed truce. Nobody expects
Lavars so-called retrenchments to

main long after the effects OF the
sedatives have passed. Balancing OF
the budget while revenues are still
shrinking rapidly and cuts IN gov
ernment expenditures are more lmag-
mary than real, is an illusion. The
French franc will remain vulnerable

ternational currencieS has been real

measure to safeguard it. And re-
gardless of the pious hopes so fire.
ouently expressed by Washington and
London with fingers crossed, stabil-
ization for long time to come ap-
pears to be but the f1gment OF a
dream.


Lull Before Storm.


The political tenseness of today Is
the lull before the storm. Left and
right groups are watching each other
closely for a false move-an incident
which will give a strategic advantage
before carrying the fight to the coun-
try or before the people at the polls.


The most dramatic element in the
French picture naturally is the in
ternal political situation. Both ends
the Left and Right parties-are
closing in on the center. For years
the Radical Socialists-the middle
road party of Edouard Herriot and
Edouard Daladier-have been the
dominating group in Parliament.
Leon Blum's Left Socialists, the sec
ond largest group. have held the bal

ferring to influence the policies of
those in office to taking the response
bility. With the death of the veteran
Socialist, Pierre Renaudel. extremists

control of the Left Socialist organiza-

Herriot, always powerful co-leader

the helm when the Stavisky scandals

particularly Daladier and Camille
Chautemps. Now that whitewash and
time have softened that menace, the
Radical old guard is reasserttng it
self. Before October Herriot will
step down and out as the Radical
whip. He has publicly announced
that he will not be candidate for lead
ership when Parliament convenes.

that Herriot will have to leave Laval's
cabinet, perhaps precipitating a new
crisis.


Alliance Denounced.


The Radical Socialist alliance-real

parties always combine against the
Conservative and Communist candi-

was denounced officially when Herriot

Common Front" with the Com

normally the big middle-path group

great forest fire swept over a heavily

shaken by successive earthquakes Even
while walls still were falling, tremors
still being felt. the community began the
task of rebuilding The disaster was
accepted without complaint. its losses
charged of" with philosophic resigna-

John r. NESBIT, son of the late
Wilbur D. Nesbit, newspaper man
and poet, recalled yesterday how his
father happened to write one of the
better known flag poems. Your Flag
and My Flag" which was recited year
after year. up and down the country,
by the late Representative from Con-
necticut, Tom Reilly.


Wilbur Nesbit. writing column for
the old Cleveland Plain Dealer. had
yen for railroad travel. One of his
best friends was the late Billy Loves,
general passenger agent for the Balti-
more & Ohio.


Tell you what. Billy" Nesbit said.
I'll write you poem In exchange for
a pass over the lines"


In the days of the railroad pass for
newspaper men. Nesbit got the pass
and wrote Your Flag and My Flag"
Years later, the poem became popular.
was set to music, and had all sorts
Of success, though Nesbit never re-
ceived penny for this only pay
the pass.


Then, woman in Richmond, Ohio,
going through the effects of her de-
ceased husband. found a manuscript
of Your Flag and My Flag" thought
her husband had written it, had it
copyrighted, and sued Wilbur Nesbit,
the author, for $4,000 damages for
plagiarism.


Nesbit. calling on Billy Loves, got
the original copyright, in his own
name, which pre-dated the Ohio
copyright by eight years, and entered
a counter suit. He won, and collected
$4,000.


That" said Nesbit, "is the first big
money any patriotic poem ever made"
So he took his entire family to
Europe.

NAVAL AIR STATION, NORTH
ISLAND. Calf, April 15.-CruiseTs OF
the air, the Navy's big patrol airplanes
here and at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii

some spectacular stunts during the
naval maneuvers in the North Pacific
next month.


Since the Macon disaster these big
patrol planes have become the sky
queens in so far as naval problems and
maneuvers are concerned.


There are seven squadronS under
the command of Rear Admiral Alfred
w. Johnson. commander of the base
force aircraft, United States Fleet.


One patrol wing, embracing two OF
these squadrons. each squadron hav-
ing six planes. operates with the base
force aircraft flagship Wright, which
moves with the fleet.

Pearl Harbor, has five squadrons, two
of six big patrol planes each, and three
with IL slightly smaller patrol planes
each. The third wing is at the Pan
anna Canal.


Plans for the fleet maneuvers are
secret. Rear Admiral Johnson and his
fliers, however, have been studying
charts of the 100000 square miles
of maneuver grounds, which embrace
the Pacific Coast, Alaska and the
Hawaiian Islands. 1t is quite likely
all boundaries of the area will be
touched by the big air patrols, prob
ably with some new record-breaking
flights.

Hawaii to the Philippines after the
maneuvers is reported to be under con-
sideration.

CHICAGO, February 16EThe
menace Of a dangerous Spring food
down the Mississippi Valley lies
laten in the northern woods and
plains.


January SHOWS and rains, from the
headwaters in Minnesota to the
Louisiana Delta, were double the
usual fall in some regions and
preparations already have been made
to speed aid If the flood menace
strikes.


No immediate peril has been
sighted. Nevertheless, Government
officers said today protracted thaw
would send a heavy burden Of ice
and water downstream, swell tribu-
taries, broaden the Mississippi and
jeopardize the lowlands.


Three powerful agencies have or
ganized to spot the danger in ad-
vance and are ready to provide
prompt aid If needed. Representa-
tives of the United States Weather
Service and Coast Guard and the
Red Cross formulated their program
last week at q conference in Evans
vile, Ind.


Coast Guard headquarters at Chi
cago have devised scheme for rush
ing help to the stricken regions. -Four
hours after the receipt of orders they
can have 30 motorized sur: boats
aboard fiat cars and headed for the
flood scene. The Cleveland division
can dispatch nine more with equal
speed.


Upon reaching the inundated ter
ritory, the 36-foot boats would be
launched and each manned by an
ofiicer and two men. Portable radio
sets at strategic points would guide
the rescue craft as they chug through
the waters to bring stranded resi-
dents to safety. Meteorologists would
survey the situation and issue warn
inRA.

By the Associated Press.


DETROIT, August 8.--Jean Miller,
accused in scathing cross-examination
Of acting" during her trial for the
murder of Howard Carter Dickinson.
slipped from the witness chair and
fell on her face in Recorders Court
today.


A half-hour recess was taken while
the former burlesque house dancer,
on trial with three other self-styled
cocktail bar racketeers" for the slay-
ing of the New York attorney, was
treated by physician who said she
was suffering from hysteria.


Judge Issues Edict.


Sharp exchanges between counsel
led Judge John A. Boyne to issue an
edict against "snickering, Sneering and
smiling" by court officers.


The order was issued after one of
the defense staff had protested that
an investigator for the prosecutors
Office was smiling" during the Miller
woman's testimony.


She declared in direct examination
that she had been coached by Police
Sergt. Earl Switzer and Detective
Earl Branton when she made her
final statement to the prosecutor in
which she admitted that she, William
Lee Ferris, and Loretta and Florence
jackson, enticed Dickinson to accom-
pany them on the ride which ended
in his Staying here June 26.


Tells of Promise.


"You can say anything and 1t
won't count unless you sign it," she
testified Switzer had told her. She
said she had been promised that she
would be only State witness in the
trial of the other three defendants.


In concluding her direct testimony
she denied she had anything to do
with the murder of Dickinson, who
was a nephew of Chief Justice
Charles Evans Hughes.


Prosecutor Duncan c. McCrea
opened cross examination with the
"acting" charge, which was immedi-
ately followed by the dancers fall
from the stand.

FREDERICKSBURG, Va, April
26.-A 32.year-old farm woman,
who, witnesses say. aged 80 years
in appearance during her four
months employment by Stafford
county farmer, brought the arrest
last night of the farmer on assault
charges.


Mrs. Sophia Brooks, gray haired
and haggard, who friends could
hardly recognize as the same
healthy, buxom girl they had seen
during the winter, made charges
Of brutality which caused the ar.
rest of Frank Hart, 33, former
Stafford county deputy sheriff.


Assault and Battery


Mrs. Brooks, a young widow,
charged that during the time she
worked at Harris farm, she was
beaten and starved and forced to
live in the same room with col
ored youth. Hart was charged
with assault and battery.


Earlier in the week Mrs. Brooks
went to the home of neighborS
Of, Hart in Stafford county and
pleaded for help. She said she
had escaped after being locked in
an clubhouse for three days, with
out any comforts. Then she told
of the horrors which she claimed
had aged her 80 years in four
months.


She had gone to Harris farm
In midwinter to work for So a
week and keep.


Began Beating Her


After a short time, she said,
Hart began beating her and re-
fused to pay her.


Long hours of hard work-chop-
ping wood, feeding animals, doing
heavy manual labor-soon under.
mined her health, she stated. She
was given little food and when she
complained she was beaten unmer.
cifully. Mrs. Brooks told neighbors.


When she was sent to the Sal
walton Army home in this city.
word of her charge reached the
ears of Judge Frederick Coleman.
Last night Constable w. T. Sulli-
van arrested Hart.

ANNAPOLIS, July 19.-Coach
Charles Walsh and several MILDLY
assistants "re working with q
promising squad of Navy plebe
oarsmen this summer, a number
of whom are of the type from
which the power houses of win
ming PoughkeepSie crews are
formed.


Navy people are just about
convinced that while they may
form fine sprint crews with the
material which the crew squad

full men are needed by crews

mile grind on the Hudson.


It is pointed out that the Navy,
with an excellent crew, was
beaten last year by California
and Washington, and this year

Cornell, all crews averaging from
8 to IL pounds more than the
Nays.


Big Men Available


Fortunately, some big men
came out for rowing last year and
will be available for the varsity
squad next season. This summer
there are number of the same
kind-youths ranging from 1875
pounds to well over 200, but these,
of course, will not be ready for
the big squad until another year.


BY the season of 1887, just
after the Olympic year, unfortu.
nately, Coach Walsh should have
plenty of the biggest and strong
est type of oarsmen, and with the
big classes which are entering the
Academy, a continuance of ma
terial in abundance may be ex-
pected.


After furnishing an Olympic
winner and four crews which
finished first in the varsity event
at Poughkeepsie, the Navy is not
satisfied with crews which do not
take their share of the supreme
honorS. The material which the
last entering classes have fur.
nished revives the hope that the
Navy may take its former place
in college rowing.


Last years plebe class, now the
third, will furnish a quartet Of
big lads to the varsity squad Of
next season. They are Arthur
Yeates, George Whiteside, Carl
Fleps and George Francis. There
are several others, not so hefty.
including Paul Schultz, who pulled
we'll at stroke during the season.


Former Plebes


Yeates, WhiteSide and Fleps
rowed on the plebe crew at
Poughkeepsie. Francis rowed with
the Syracuse freshmen in 1884,
and so was not eligible for the
Navy plebeS last season. YeateS
weighs 1872 pounds, Whiteside and
Fleps about 1876 each, and Francis
over 200. Such men, Navy people
think, look well in the waist of
a varsity eight.


Careful instruction is now being
given the candidates from the new
plebe class. Four crews have been
formed and will race for the inter-
company championship early in
August. Then a representative
crew will be formed from the best
men in the four boats and will
work together for a couple Of
weeks, probably having a race with
an outside crew. It will be fine
preparation for the spring season.

Thy figure floats along.


Seekst thou the plashy brink
Of weedy lake, marge of river wide
Or where the rocking pillows rise and sink


On the chafed ocean-side?


There is Power whose
Teaches thy way along that painless coast
The desert and iimtabe air


Lone wandering, but not lost.

BOURN EMOUTH, England,
June 5 G.N.SD.-With six stab
wounds in her chest, the body of
Mrs. Alma Victoria Rattenbury,
central figure in England's "Sny.
der-Gray" mallet murder case, lay
in the Bournemouth morgue to-
day.


She committed suicide by stab
bling herself and plunging into the
lonely River Stour last night-a
few hours after she was released
from a London nursing home
where she went for a rest follow
ing her acquittal on charges of
numbering her wealthy, aged hus-
band.


The humiliation of the trial and
the fact her 19-year-old chauffeur
lover, who was convicted by the
same court that freed her, faces
the hangman'S moose on June 10
was held responsible for her sui
eide.


A post mortem examination was
understood to have revealed Mrs.
Rattenbury died of the stab
wounds in her chest. several Of
which were said to have pierced
her heart.


William Charles Mitchell, cow
man, saw her sit down by the
river bank late last night. She
took off her coat, a dagger glis-
tened for a moment in the moon
light, and then she slipped into
the black waters.

TACOMA, Wash, July 13.-Scores
nursed hurts from rocks, rife butts,
slaves and bayonets today after riot
Gus street fighting precipitated by the
prolonged Pacific Northwest lumber
strike. Six persons were seriously in
jured before National Guardsmen
quelled with tear and nausea gas a
melee in which nearly 1000 strike
sympathizers participated for four
hours.


At least 40 OF the demonstrators
were arrested and hustled of in Ma
tional Guard trucks, while scores
more. including sympathizers and
spectators, were affected by the gas
which flooded the Federal Building
and adjacent Office structures.


National Guard forces. ordered here
by Gov. Clarence D. Martin several
weeks ago. guarded today against fur
ther outbreaks.


The rioting began when big crowd
attempted to push by National
GuardSmen across the Eleventh street
bridge. leading from the business dis
trict to the mill area.


Troubles of lesser kind also
spotted" the strike picture in other
Western Washington cities. but oper-
ators asserted the strike was nearing
an end.


The striking union demanded rec
ognition, a 40-hour work week and
wage increases.

Tiger Tiger burning bright,
In the forests of the night,
What immortal hand eye
Could frame thy fearful symmetry?
In what distant deeps skies
Burnt the fire of thine eyes?
On what wings dare he aspire?
What the hand dare seize the fire?
And what shoulder, and what art,
Could twist the sinews of thy heart?
And when thy heart began to beat,
What dread hand and what dread feet?



When the stars threw down their spears,
And watered heaven with their tears,
Did He smile His work to see?
Did He who made the Lamb, make thee?
Tiger! Tiger burning bright,
In the forests of the night
What immortal hand eye

Public galleries in the Senate were
cleared for the first time in many
years today after the Senate had been
unable to find its sergeant at arms to
maintain order.


Senator Pittman, Democrat, of
Nevada, president pro tempore of the
Senate. ordered the public galleries
cleared when Senator Robinson,
Democratic leader, complained debate
could not be heard.


A few minutes earlier. the Senate
had suspended business while attend
ants searched for Chesley w. Jurney
sergeant at arms. but he could not be
located.


Actually, the complaint at that time
was that Senators themselves were
making too much noise, and Jurney
was sent for to make Senators keep
quiet.


When the confusion continued
however. Pittman suddenly ordered
that the public galleries be cleared.


His order did not include the pri-
vate gallery filled with spectators spe-
cially invited by Senators nor the
press gallery. in which the newspaper
correspondents were reporting the
proceedings.

bers, and their antics are relatively
unimportant, but Tommy "Bozo"
Snyder, who brings his Blue Rhythm
Girls" to the Gayety this week, Ger
tainly does not fall in this class.


His inimitable tomfoolery in pam
tomime, which places him right up
at the top among the few really good
burlesque funsters. is displayed this
week in that theater scene, wherein
he sits in the audience" of theater
within a theater and disrupts every
thing and everybody in sight, and

Coleman's top hat with bags of pea
nuts. In a new skit, "Bozo" plays

spite of the Snyder competition, man
age to get across some really funny
skits. Don Trent and Bob Roberts
take the straight roles and split the
singing assignments, doing both very
well.

are Gertrude Hayes, Billie Hughes,
Dolores Green and June and Margie
White, which is a very acceptable
group of feminine charmerS. Most
approved last night was Miss Hughes,
who has a voice shade on the per-
simmon side, but who also has more
winning personality than any one else
present, and the knack of capturing
the audiences favor. Miss Hayes
helps no little in putting the comedy
into the comedy scenes, being one OF
the best Soubrettes to play the Ninth
street house in a long, long time.

probably easier on the eyes than most

NEW YORK, June 22.-The stock
market continued to push forward
in today's brief session and many new
highs for the year were recorded.
Week end realizing in the FIRST hour
was overcome with little dtfnculty and
bullish activity broadened later. The
close was firm. Transfers approx
mated GOO, 900 shares.


Optimism apparently ruled In the
boardrooms and profit taking was not
urgent at any time. Strength was dis
played by few specialties, but the
general gains ranged from fractions to
around point. Washington develop
ments, on the whole, did not seem to
disturb sentiment.


Shares Of air reduction and Ameri-
can Can got up more than points
each and American Tobacco "B" and
Allied Chemical were nearly as much
higher. Other advances were regis
tered by Du Pont, Safeway Stores,
Montgomery Ward, Chrysler, General
Motors, Philip Morris, Johns Manville,
Standard Oil of New Jersey, Kenne-
colt, American Smelling, International
Telephone, American Telephone, Con-
Solidated Gas, North American, Beth
lehem Steel and Electric Auto-Lite.
Most Of the rails and oils were I'M
changed to slightly improved.


The belief was expressed in some
quarters that, barring exceptionally
bad news, industrial activities this
Fall will be considerably ahead Of the
same 1884 period.


The thought in the financial dis
trict was that the Presidents higher
tax program may not get through
Congress this session and the opinion
was voiced that before the next term
administration forces might feel much
different about the "distribution-of-
wealth plan.


The action Of the House Interstate
Commerce Committee in shearing the
utility holding company bill bright
ened the outlook for owners Of power
loans and equities.


Announcement that retail cigarette
prices, which dropped when the
N. R. A. codes were invalidated, would
be raised next week cheered followers
of tobacco stocks.

threatened to blow the rapids dry.

river several days, backed the water
into Lake Erie and laid bare many of
the rocks in the channel between the
American shore and Goat Island in
midstream at the edge Of the falls.

in the past blown the American chan
mel nearly dry. Northeasters have
pushed the water back from the Ca
madam Horseshoe Falls and piled it
into the American section. However.
neither channel ever has been swept
clean.

Heaven bless dear Dr. Granger" thought
Sandra. 1t was thanks to him she was having
this final fling before matrimony engulfed her.
She had seemed restless and diSpirited, that

drawer at home. All the business of finding the
dear little house with its Japanese cherry and
lilac tree that waited for them and bits of
furniture picked up at sales to put in it.


Send her away by herself for rest and
change, the doctor had said. do her good.


Heaven bless him." murmured Sandra
again.


She walked along the deck, the wind blow
ing out the soft flounces of her frock and max
ing her look for all the world like woodland
fairy.


The young man in his chair in the corner

crimson shawl did not draw his eye from his
book


Sandra was not accustomed to being over
looked. 1t made her angry. Il haven't" she
told herself, comfortingly, really got down
to him yet"


There was dancing on deck that night.
There, far off, stood Nigel Raynor looking on.
1t was, said Sandra, cruel waste. Her eyes
as she passed him in another man. arms said,
Won't you?" Her wide red mouth smiled
eager invitation.


But when she passed that way again. his
place was empty. The preposterous fellow had
simply gone to bed. The glamour went out of

Did the old charm that had never failed her
not work any more? Was her power of attrac-

smiled, most men smiled back again, and we're
pleased about it. This person went to bed!


Later, seated on her bunk in blue silk

been fun to teach the inaccessible young man

plenty of other nice young men on the ship.
The First Officer had very experienced

the fold?


She wrote her evening bulletin to Berkeley.

keen on it, and came early to bed. l have had
another and closer look at the inaccessible
young man. have come to the conclusion he
isn't really worth worrying about. But there is

awfully nice man who is going to the Soudan."

DUKA PUKA is odd among the
l islands of the world. Its natives
are going native"


One of the most favored of the
glamorous South Sea Islands, Puka
Puka. an atoll with a lagoon and
sandy beaches fringed with palms, was
picked as paradise by white settlers
who established there a trading post
and coconut estates. But since the
depression the white settlers have
abandoned their enterprises and left
for home. Now the natives are re-
verting to their former ;tyle CT living
The grass skirt and the loin cloth are
taking the place Of the calico Mother
Hubbard and the denim trousers, the
coconut-oil lamp is supplanting that
which burned kerosene, and the ma
tives are using shell hooks for fishing
instead of steel ones. Tea, bread and
canned meat are being discarded for
native food.

On the hurricane-swept Florida keys
has been enacted the final episode OF the
tragedy of The Bonus MarcherS.


The men died as they had lived, help
less orphans of the storms. The light
ning-lit madness of war tore them loose
from the relative simplicity and security
of the slow-moving age into which they
had been born. When the cannon ball
storm had passed over the desolated
fields of the earth they were blown
into a fast strange postwar world by
the initiating breezes of hero worship.
These subsidized and they found the calm
uncomfortable. After a brief lull they
were torn loose from whatever security
they had been able to find by the blasts
of the great depression. Again they were
blown hither and yon-great numbers
of them into the miasmic tln-can
CITY of the AnacoStia fats. which WASH
ington remembers so we'll And now
the hurricane, blowing them to death
and the peace of the great darkness 1t
was the last act for them of the drama
which opened with the bugle blasts OF
1917 The immediate responsibility Tor
the shambles probably will be fixed by
the investigations already ordered. But
one cannot escape the thought that the
real cause lies beyond the reach of any
Investigator. They were the victims OF
a hurricane sweeping the earth, whose
path no meteorologist can forecast nor
understand.


It was the tragedy of these men-and
perhaps the tragedy of all of us-to be
born into an age of hurricanellke tram
sition such as history has not known.
Life demanded of them a rapid series
of establishments which they were not
equipped by nature to make. Conse-
uuently they made them clumslly and
with infinite pain. They were bona f1de
veterans of the Great War. 1t was prob
ably responsible, in large part, for their
inadequacy. They deserved well OF their
country. Some of them were the victims
of material wounds, for which they were
given a small measure of compensation.
But these men and many others were
the victims of spiritual wounds and dis
abilities for which the Veterans Admin
istration mails no checks, but which
may well have been more serious, so
far as adjustment was concerned. than
any physical injuries they could have
suffered.


Some men came out of the war with
wrecked bodies-limping, staggering and
coughing their way into the security OF
peace. Some men came out, on. the
other hand, in far better physical shape
than before. Even SO, some men
stripped off their olive drab and donned
the store-clothes uniforms of civilian
life more self reliant and capable of adj
justment than on the day they first
subscribed to the articles Of war, and
some came back far less adequate than
before for any self-directed coping with
the multiplying complexities of living.
Among the latter were many OF these
poor victims of the hurricane.


Storm-t tossed they lived. Storm-tossed
they died, leaving an economically and
spiritually storm-tossed world behind
them.

AUBURNDALE. Mass. February 16
N).-Commodity prices for the week
ending February is successfully
climbed to new high in the broad
upswing in commodity prices which
has been in force for practically two
years. The movement was not gen.
eral, but again definitely due to the
agricultural and live stock groups.
During the week only four advances
were recorded, namely, agricultural
products, live stock. fine textiles and
vegetable oils. Only one group de-
clined and this was of very limited
character. All other groupS-nine in
number-maintained sidewise course
recording no price fluctuations from
the previous week.


Industrial prices moved sidewise,
the latest index holding under the
average reached in January. Indus
trial activity has experienced difficulty
in moving upward but the aggregate
volume has held at favorable plane
in view of the uncertainty over the
gold clause decision.


Farm Prices Higher.


Agricultural prices gained some
ground, now close to the high reached
in January. During the week higher
quotations were noted for wheat. corn,
oats, barley, rye, beans and f1axseed.
Fractional declines occurred in eggs,
butter and potatoes.


Live stock prices again dominated
commodity markets by recording an
other broad increase, establishing the
index at new high. Compared with
the base year 1926, all commodities
stand at 1874, industrial 72.6, agri-
cultural TIA, with live stock the high
est of all, 77.9. This is a tremendous
contrast from year ago During the
week all items-cattle, hogs, sheep
and lambs-participated in the ex-
tended price recovery.


Non-ferrouS metals represented the
only group to decline and this was of
limited scope due to a break In the
spot price of tin under the so per cent
level which more than counteracted
slight strength in lead and silver.


Fine Textiles Rise.


Fine textiles were slightly higher
than the previous week, entirely due
to moderate price strength in raw
silk


Vegetable oils recorded a marked
price increase under the impetus of

TERRE HAUTE, Ind, July %
0.NSO The backbone of In
diana'S first general strike was
broken by 1000 National Guards
men here today.


While militiamen roamed the
city streets in automobiles with
rifles and machine guns at
ready angle, merchants, factory
owners and other business men
resumed their normal activities in
increasing numbers.


The paralysis, which settled
upon this city of nearly $4,000
population when general strike
was called in sympathy with
workers of the Columbian Enamel
ing and Stamping Company, was
relieved considerably.
Transportation Crippled


Only a few restaurants and
drug stores were open early today
but during the day clothing stores,
the Terre Haute Brewing Com.
pany, and a few factories began
to operate. Milk, ice and bread
deliveries, however, were still miss
ing and there were no street cars,
buses or taxicabs operating.


The Merchants Association
voted to reopen their stores at
once, The merchants believed
that with the State troops on
duty shops and stores could be
opened with safety.


Injured in Fight


State soldiers were the targets
of bricks and stones when they
entered premises of the Column
bian Company here early today,
but they did not fire on the riot
ers. Instead. city police hurled
tear-gas bombs and the militia
men with fixed bayonets. drove
the crowd back and arrested five
persons who allegedly hurled the
missiles.


One State trooper and a mem.
Der of the crowd were injured
slightly during the melee.


Brig. Gen. D. Wray Deprez,
commander of the State troops
predicted that practically all in
dustrial, commercial and trans
portation activities of the city
would be resumed before night
fall.


Clerks Ready to Return


He was handicapped in his ef-
forts to restore normal conditions
by the fact that the Terre Haute
Star, the only morning news
paper, failed to publish an edition
for the first time since it was
founded in 1908.


General Deprez used radio sta
ton WIDOW here to broadcast a
message to business men and citi-
zens that they could renew their
everyday activities in safety.


Clerks crowded the sidewalks in
front of the stores waiting for
the word to take their places be.
hind the counters again.

Editor, McGill Commodity Service. Inc,


Auburndale Mass.


AUBURNDALE, Mass, December 7
Commodity prices during the
first week of December climbed up
ward, reaching the highest point since
early October. Price trends were
mixed, as out of IA individual groups
four averaged higher, five declined
and five remained unchanged. A
check-up shows that the higher price
level was due primarily to two groups
namely, live stock and agricultural
products. In both instances prices
advanced substantially over the No
vember average, but held under the
high points reached in October.


Industrial prices moved downward,
falling well under the November
average. Industrial activity is be-
ginning to stabilize, following a sub
stantial seasonal upswing. The latest
estimate of business activity stands at
Is per cent under normal.


Farm Prices Strong.


Agricultural prices were strong, al
though more items declined than ad-
vanced. Lower quotations as COM
pared with a week ago for corn. bar
ley, rye, cotton, beans and potatoes
were more than offset by higher levels
for butter, flaXseed, wool and eggs.


Live stock, the third major group,
registered the most extensive advance
of any group, rejecting higher quota
tions for cattle, hogs and sheep.


Non-ferrous metal prices declined
moderately, principally due to a de-
cline in tin.


Paint materials were also lower,
caused by lower markets for roSin,
turpentine and china wood oil.


Fine textiles represent the third
group to advance. Price strength in
wool more than offset the lower quo
tations recorded for cotton and raw
silk.


Coarse textiles, however, were lower
under the leadership Of burlap and
hemp, which averaged under the level
of week ago.


Hide and leather prices also were
lower, as packer hide quotations
reached the 14a4 cent level and GER
tain finished feathers as well were
off slightly.


Vegetable Oils Gain.


Vegetable oils moved upward as
coconut, corn and cottonseed oils ad-
vanced. China wood oil represents
the only item in this group to decline.

during the past six weeks, gen.
orally wearing a simple grey flan.
mel costume and cape. She fire.
quently dimes at the principal

holm.


In this respect she acts far diff
ferently than she usually does

with the others at her dinner
parties, she watches those on the
floor intently and fully enters into
the spirit of table fun.

ANNAPOLIS, Sept. 9.-NaVy
football gets under way this week
for the 1885 season. Two weeks
ago, the coaching staff assembled
at the Naval Academy, and the
varsity will find a strong and
well-organized plebe team ready
to give it plenty of work in the
early lineups.


The coaching staff, under the
director of football, Commander
John H. Brown, and Head Coach
Tom Hamilton, have been hold
ing daily conferences and the
work of the season is we'll out
lined. Scrimmages against the
plebe team will start in about
two weeks.


The coaches propose a stiff
routine to break in the rather
green players who must fill the
positions vacated by seven regu-
lars lost by graduation. Included
in the latter are the two great
backs, Buzz Berries and Bill
Clark, and five Of the forwards
who started against the Army
last fall.


Ball Carriers Needed


The remaining backs are Tom
my King and Dick Pratt, reli-
able all-around players, but not
outstanding ball carriers. There
fore one of the big problems of
Tom Hamilton and Johnny Will
son will be to develop some ball
carriers and punters to take the
places, as we'll as possible, Of
Berries and Clark.


The possibilities in the carrying
line are Snead Schmidt, Ned
Thomas, Charley Manning and Fay
Willsie, Of last years squad, and
Young Bill Ingram, Bolton Crab
bit) Rankin and Bob Antrim,
who came up from last years
plebe eleven. Severa other
plebes may develop as the season
progresses.


Only one change will be made
in the varsity coaching staff from
last year. Tom Hamilton, who
steered the Navy team to its first
victory over the Army in 10 years,
is again the helm as head coach.
Johnny Wilson will be the back
field coach, and Edgar (Rip) Mil
Ter and Johnny Cross, will look
after the line candidates.


Byng Coaches Ends


Yves Byng will succeed Oscar
Hagberg as coach of the ends.
Byng entered the Acamedy from
Washington and is one Of the
Navy's great general athletes, hav-
ing won major letters in football,
basketball and baseball. Byng
played with Hamilton on the
West Coast Navy team and later
coached it. He graduated from
the Navay Academy in 1881. How
ard Caldwell will be head coach
of the plebes, and Frank Foster of
B Squad.


The Navy opens the season at
Annapolis on Sep e mber %
against William and Mary. The
Indians always give the Navy
team a hard battle and the game
should give a good line on what
the coaches have been able to do
toward moulding a strong Navy
team from. green material.

TOXIC. January 3l-Fresh hos
tilities between Mongols and Japa-
nese and Manchouquan cavalry were
reported today along Manchoukuo'S
frontier bordering outer Mongolia.


Dispatches from Hsinking, Man
choukuo, to the Rengo (Japanese)
News Agency, said the cavalry detach-
ment was pursuing band of Mongols
fleeing across the frozen steppes in
80 below zero temperature.


The pursuing force was reported
to have pressed on after capturing
Kalkha Mao. the big Lamaist temple
northeast of Bor Nor.


japanese general headquarters an
nounced that japanese cavalry was
participating. Its purpose, the an
nouncement said, was to "expel in
vading Mongols from Manchoukuo."


Although no Soviet troops were re-
ported involved in the fighting, OH
cial japanese circles generally regard
the outer Mongolian government as
under Moscow's domination. Japa-
nese military spokesmen called atten-
ton to the fact that reports that the
Japanese had invaded" Mongolia
emanated from the Soviet capital.


The Japanese contend that the ter
ritory in which troops were active is
part of Manchoukuo.


A spokesman for the Japanese war
Office declared the military operations
signified no intention Of permanently
occupying Mongolian territory.


The japanese army hopes, the COM
munique said, to make further fight
ing unnecessary through negotiations
with the Mongols. Peaceful measures
failing, however, the communique in
dicated, all force necessary would be
used.

~ ATEWAY for countless gall

years ago, but almost ignored
~ in modern times, Mexico's
Rip Van Wrinkle port, Acapulco, now
is waking to renewed activity. The
largest liners plying between New York
and California plan to call there next
year to drop tourists for Mexico City.


Sleepy Acapulco, on the Pacific. has
one Of the finest natural harbors in
the world, says a bulletin from the
Washington, D. c., headquarters OF
the National Geographic Society
which describes the quiet little tropical
town thus:


Acapulco is a crescent Of pastel
colored, adobe cubicles, topped by tiny
patches of red tile roofs, and occasional
green coconut palms. A few buildings,
taller or broader, stand out from the
mass of one-storied dwellings-church.
town hall and jail, covered market
building and sprinkling of consulates
and hotels. The narrow winding
streets are rarely crowded. Heat makes
the air sticky, like hot fiy-paper," but
visitors endure the climate to enjoy
the towns tropical beauty.


Behind it rise the steep, cactus-cov-
cred Sierra Madres. which have
throttled Acapulco's progress like chok-
ing fingers.


CORTES used its magnificent har-
- Dor in 1881. A hilly, half-mile-
wide peninsula between bay and ocean
forms a natural breakwater, offering
about square miles of placid, almost
land-locked shelter within earshot of
Pacific breakers pounding against the
rocky headlands outside.


BY 1850 trade at the port supported
little village, which the Spanish forti-
fed with the grim gray fort of San
Diego. still glowering above one tip
of the town.


The Aztec name for the settle
ment-Acapulco. place where the
reeds abound''-was borne on trade
winds around the world. Galleons
from the Far East brought fragrant
cargoes of gums and spice, of dark
cotton prints and rice from India.
rich brocaded silks from Japan, ex-
quisite porcelains from China. Occa
sional slavers discharged their human
cargoes to work nearby sugar plan
tations. and legend claims that one
brought a kidnapped princess, whose
popularity is commemorated in the
national Mexican girls fiesta dress,
the China Poblana costume of green
bordered red skirt, loose white en-
broidered blouse and gay shawl.

Orient journeyed inland over the
tortuous rocky "Camino Real" a brig
and-infested mountain trail to Mex
leo, D. F., and thence to Veracruz
for reshipment to Spain. Transport
was by strings of burros. or by slow

gin until Monday. The Senate's

The Capital was back at work to-
day after a quiet Thanksgiving-and
badly battered turkeys we're in family
ice chests, awaiting second appear
ance.


A cold, heavy rain, starting about
the time thousands were making their
way from church. kept good part
of the city indoors after the dinner
hour, but despite this, foot ball games,
races and motion pictures, principal
items on the entertainment program,
were well patronized.


Officialdom was scattered from such
widely separated points as Warm
Springs, were President Roosevelt pre-
sided at the Thanksgiving board, to
Wake Island, a dot in the Pacific,
where Secretary of War Dern and Mrs.
Dern passed the day.


Party at White House.


The White House was alight, how
ever. The Presidents daughter, Mrs.
Anna Roosevelt Boettiger, with her
husband, entertained small party.
The principal celebration was at the
Willard Hotel, the Navy relief ball
having as honor guests Secretary of
the Navy and Mrs. Swanson.


The annual Pan-American mass at
st. Patrick's Church brought out
many members of the diplomatic corps
from the Southern countries, and
afterward the distinguished guests
were entertained at luncheon by the
pastor, Msgr. Cornelius F. Thomas.


. Unforgetable for Derns.


Secretary and Mrs. Dern had an
unforgetable day. En- route home from
the Philippines on the cruiser Ches-
ter. they put in at Wake Island, where
before only one white woman-wife of
a member of the air base installation
crew-had ever landed. The base is
maintained by Pan-American Airways
for its San Francisco Manila service,
and the only inhabitants are the crew.
A radio to the War Department told
of the event. The China Clipper,
winging by from Guam to Manila,
brought in the "makings" for the din
ner, which included turkey, fresh to-
matoes and ice cream.


Hundreds of persons were fed by
relief agencies here and representa-
tives of the Animal Protective Asso-
citation went through alleys and
around dumps, leaving food for stray
dogs and cats. Crumbs also were put
out for birds.

Spain first reigned over the

Great Britain has ruled the waves

In this new contest among the
nations, even as in the maritime
struggle, supremacy in the aerial
trade lanes will be established
by high-speed merchant ships of
the air, long-distance flying boats.


The United States believes itself
a leader in commercial aviation
and hopes to win major prizes in
this great international race.

SAN FRANCISCO, April 9
UN.SD.-Heavy loss of life and
millions of dollars in property
damage lay today in the wake of
the worst California storm in re-
cent years.


Nine men in a Southern Paci-
fic section crew were killed when
their motor railway car crashed
head-on with a gravel train.
Three others in the crew were
injured and another was reported
dying.


The crew had been repairing
O section of roadbed between
Roseville and Marysville which
had been washed out by the
storm.


Judge Feared Dead


Eight other persons were def
nitely known to have lost their
lives in swollen rivers and traffic
accidents throughout the State.
Another possible victim, Judge
Gus Schiller, of Woodland, was
missing. It was feared he drowned
when a boat overturned at Sacra-
mento.


After raging two days, the storm
apparently had abated in north
ern California, and was moving
Eastward over Nevada.


Damage in Central California
was appalling. Miles of property
was under two and three feet of
water. Orchards still in bloom suf-
fered heavily Scores were driven
from their homes, and livestock
marooned. Rivers roads were
closed.


Thrilling R6Bcues


Numerous thrilling rescues were
reported. Fifteen transients we're
saved from shed roofs when 10 feet
of water flooded the Sacramento
River district "jungles."


A mile of rack near Marysville on
the Southern Pacific was washed
out. It was this section workers
were repairing when their truck
crashed headon into a gravel
train.


While the storm damage was
estimated in the millions of dol
lars, Major E. H. Bowie, district
Federal weather forecaster here,
said the record-breaking rains ulti-
mately will be of inestimable
value.


Three dead was the storm toll
IN Southern California.

HANKOW, China Sunday, July
14.-Swarms Of coolies today strength
ened dikes which threaten to open and
loose the raging Yangtse River on
the city.


Leaks have opened in places, and
the river waters have penetrated to
the heart of the city, driving the resi-
dents to upper floors and filling them
with fear that the flood embellishments
cannot long stand. Refugees, sur
rounded by their chattels, are huddled
In the center Of the city.


Dykes protecting the neighboring
city of Hanyang-a metropolis Of more
than 10000 inhabitants-flnally gave
way today before the ceaseless batter
ing Of the Han River. and the city
lay half submerged under the weight
Of millions Of tons of muddy water.


The frantic populace fed. Only a
small section of the city escaped in
undation. Homeless residents were
streaming across the river into Han
kow as rapidly as the available boats
could carry them.


A heat wave over the Yangtse Valley
added to the suffering of the terrified
people.


Rain. accompanied by hail, at Lam
chow, Kansu Province, converted
mountain streams to torrents which
destroyed roads and crops. These
streams feed the already swollen river,
now raging through Shensi Province.


Heavy rains are reported at Kaifeng
Honan Province, adding to the food
danger Of the Yellow River West
Shantung is overrun with floods pour
ing southeastward along the Grand
Canal


At Kiukiang, the Yanztse reached
| its highest point since 1870, at 456
feet. Its volume is increased by the
vast inflow from the Han River and
Tungting Lake, which have devastated
the country surrounding them.


The death toll and property damage
are incalculable. Floating bodies are
not an uncommon sight throughout
the stricken region.

LORAIN, Ohio, June 22-Common
Pleas Judge Guy B. Findley issued an
injunction against the Cleveland
Newspaper Guild late yesterday, pro-
hibiting picketing by more than two
members at the Lorain Journal and
restraining publication of any matter
designed to intimidate Journal en-
ployeS, advertisers or subscribers.


The injunction was requested by
the newspaper after its managing edi-
tor, Frank Malloy, was assaulted by
unidentified persons as he entered the
newspapers plant yesterday.


Members of the guild and sympath-
Izers have been picketing the journal
plant since controversy between the
management and editorial employees
arose last week.


The injunction forbids members Of
the guild from interfering in any way
with the employees entering or leaving
the Journal plant, from interfering
with truck drivers or carriers and
from lettering near the plant, except
for two members, who are permitted
to be stationed there.


The guild members are enjoined
against the use of threats for purposes
of boycotting the paper. The injunc-
ton further provides that they shall
not intimidate advertisers by threat
ening to boycott their establishments
If they do not cancel advertising con-
tracts.

ST. LOUIS, February 2.-Slowly,
but with a persistence that is alarm
ing traders, professional American fur
hunters are deserting their traps.


Commission men along the st. Louis
river front, where the largest raw fur
market in the world is clustered in q
few decrepit buildings, have just fin
ished another buying season, marked
by a diminishing take" Of valuable
furs. Mink, skunk and raccoon were
short on the market this year, with
trapping in the Northwest virtually
ended for the season.


The drought, the Government farm
policy and a saturated market in fur
coats is blamed by the st. Louis buy
ers for idle traps. Animals are abun-
dant. but the trappers are gone.


Farmers with Government crop
checks laid by for the Winter have
forsaken the trap lines that occupied
them in past Winters.


''The Negro share cropper, with
cotton money in his overalls, lets his
soon dog Sleep" explained M. Lenz,
fur buyer.


The drought left deep mark on
the value of Central and Northwest
ern hides, and trappers let the ami
mails run free rather than bother
with inferior furs. Southern hides
were abundant, but brought only o
nominal price, A.

We had "processed lamb"
and "honey fox" at the ninth
Fashion Congress yesterday at
the Mayflower.


Now don't look surprised. That's
not part Of the luncheon served
at these weekly events-but just
two fashion terms. One describes
the color Of the fox which will
trim smart coats and suits this
spring-and the other-although
it sounds edible-ls lamb fur
with all the kinks taken out
leaving it flat and ready to adorn
the smarteSt frocks and wraps.


Acting as judges at the Con.
gresS, sponsored by The Washing
ton Times, were Mrs. William
Beverley Mason, Mrs. Lawrence
Groner, Mrs. Malcolm McConihe,
Mrs. John Philip Hill, Miss Julie
Dell Zimmerman, and Miss Helen
Wardman. This committee Sc
lected frocks and suits from eight
groups and awarded them their
seal of approval as practical and
attractive in design and fabric
for the average woman.


Masculine Trend


Women will steal their thunder
from masculine fashions this
spring, it seems. Such coat ideas
as are embodied in the Norfolk
jacket-the belted and shirred
back type; gabardine suiting;
coats lined with dark satin with
white lining in the sleeves, have
all been used to give the feminine
world its latest models. Capes and
neck scarfs will be the only "flut-
tering" touches to the otherwise
severe simplicity of suits and
coats. Tweeds and what were once
described as clothes for the coun-
try will walk side by side down the
avenue for street wear. The for
mality of dressier costumes need
not prevail for town wear.


Two costumes from Erlebacher
might be described as the show
favorites. One was a black ensem-
ble-a three-quarter cape and
dress of black wool crepe with a
crossbar running through it. The
cape was trimmed with the
"processed lamb" otherwise known
as Galyak. Voting was tied be-
tween this and a suit of brown
wool crepe with the same cross
bar-a three-quarter length coat
trimmed in "honey fox' and a
dress with a high neckline and
shoulder fastenings.


TweedS Shown


The rest of the showing con-
sisted in the popular tweeds.
Many checked jackets with plain
skirts were shown. From Kann's
came smart three-piece suit
gray and white checked jacket
Norfolk style-with plain gray
skirt to match coat with a swas,
ger vent in back-another mascu
line touch. With this a dark
blue linen blouse which the
judges thought too dark. They
decided a yellow blouse would be
more suitable.


From Jelleff's was a Navy blue
gabardine three-piece suit-single-
breasted jacket, yellow scarf at
the neck-and long coat lined in
black to the sleeves, which were
lined with white.


Checks may be as racy as you
like. A suit from the Hecht Com.
pany combined a navy blue skirt
with a navy blue coat which had
wide French blue crossbars. This
won the judges approval over a
three-piece suit with a scarf, cape
and belt which had too many
broken lines.

rear exit.

ambulances and police cars to an
emergency hospital where all but two
we're treated and sent home.

NEW YORK, February ls.-Now
that Wall Streets nerves have been
soothed by the Supreme Courts de-
cisions in the gold cases, business
analysts say more attention can be
paid to the country's economic picture


Notwithstanding official assurances
at various times that the Roosevelt
administration had worked out plans
to meet almost any kind of emergency
following the decision, an atmosphere
of restraint prevailed to some degree
up to the very moment of the decision.


Through all this period of uncer-
tainty, however, business activity
throughout most sections of the United
States not only maintained the mod
crate gains recorded In January, but
some lines continued to expand during
the current month, although less spec
tacularly.


Long-standing January records were
broken by motor production, which
was IS per cent higher than December
and 81 per cent greater than year
ago, with indications that February
output would even exceed this showing.
Deliveries and sales showed CORE
spondingly large gains in both this
country and abroad


Aided materially by miscellaneous
freight, which includes automobiles
and steel, car loadings on class l
railroads averaged slightly higher
during the first 5 weeks of the year,
and during the 7-day period ended
February attained the highest level
for that week since 1881.


Rising industrial activity has been
reflected in the week-to-week gains
recorded in elecGric powsr production,
and although steel output shows some
signs on leVeling off from the recently
established peak 6f better than SO per
cent of capacity, the estimates for
the current week are well ahead OF
the same period last year.


Corporation earnings reports for
1884 continue to reflect the steady
progress the majority Of compa .lies
made toward normal profits in that
year.


Durable goods industries also con-
tinue to show signs Of coming out Of
the acutely depressed state Of affairs
of the past three years.

A SIDE from the international


~ good will that will be created
~ in the meeting Of Mexico
= City's all-star high school foot
ball team with the Capitals best
public high eleven here November 30,
a sport which the neighboring nation
has striven to establish, will be given
a much-needed boost.


Made possible when the Board of
Education waived its rule against post
season games, the contest promises to
promote more good will between Mex
leo and the United States than a
treaty could.


Although the grid game has been
played by the high school teams of
Mexico City for the last four years.
foot ball has not received sufficient
concentrated attention to displace
soccer.


Game Enthuses Mexicans.


A CCORDING to dispatches from the


Latin American capital, Mexi-
cans are enthused over the impending
high school game and have rallied to
foot ball


Government officials in Mexico, real
izing that foot ball develops quick
thinking, sportsmanship and discipline
probably more than any other sport.
are anxious to have their future citi-
zens turn TO the game.


And the brawny boys of Latin
America are doing just that-despite
difficulties which have been hard to
overcome. Foremost among the hard
ships is the even climate across the
border which permits one game being
played practically the year around.
Thus the game fails to receive con-
centration at any one time.


Tough Task for Coach.
The coaching problem that was


discouraging has been solved.
Robert P. Martin. coach of the Mexi-
can al-stars. speaks nothing but Eng
lish. yet has taught foot ball to a
group of gridders who speak nothing
but Spanish, Portuguese and French.


Central and Eastern elevens, which
probably will be battling November IS
for the right to meet the Mexicans.
are both capable teams. but no doubt
could be forced to the limit to get
the nod over their dark-skinned
opponents.


But regardless of which team wins
the real victor, in a sense, will be
Mexico. 1t has taken the United
States more than half century to
develop foot ball to its present popu-
larity. Mexico promises TO take a
shorter route-with this international
high school game helping a lot.

Showers and leaden skies marred the

Washington has devoted solely to rest
and relaxation.


Many of the hopeful thousands who
had trouped to nearby beaches and
resorts for the long week end were re-
turning by noon today, disappointed

of yesterday and today had spoiled
their brief vacation.


The weather prediction locally was

neSday or Thursday.


Washington was not alone in its
Labor day weather misfortune. Rain
blanketed Pennsylvania, Maryland,
Northern Virginia and the entire mid
die section Of the country from Texas
north. although the West, New York
and New England enjoyed clear skies.
At 1890 am. today the thermometer
registered but 81 degrees, considerably
below the average for this time Of
year.

JACKSONVILLE, Fla, September
Cuba and extreme Southern
Florida kept anxious eyes today on
tropical storm which moved threat
eningly westward from the Bahamas
apparently headed for the 90-mile
water gap between Havana and Key
West.


Early today the Army Meteorologi-
cal Service in Havana said the storm
center was located about 180 miles
each of the Cuban capital and was
moving slowly westward with in
creasing intensity. Observers reported
hurricane winds near the storm
center.


Warnings Sent Out.


Expecting the storm to pass
through the channel between Havana
and Key West sometime this after
noon, Cuban forecasters warned
Havana and Mantanzas along the
north coast of the island to take
precautions against tidal waves.


A second tropical storm crossed
the coast of Mexico south Of Vera
Cruz late yesterday, sweeping the
coastline with violent winds, but ap-
parently doing no great damage.


Town Virtually Evacuated.


The New Orleans Weather Bureau
said the disturbance was of moderate
intensity and apparently was losing
most Of its force as it swept inland.
The town of Isabella Des Auga In
Santa Clara Province virtually was
evacuated last night as residents fed
to higher ground.


Key West boarded up in prepara-
ton for the storm and shipping In
the Keys and as far up the coast as
Miami took to cover.


Reports to the Colonial government
at Nassau said the Bahama Islands
escaped with minor damage when the
storm passed over Long Island and
Just below Andres Island.

Brief resumption of telegraph

Fire swept the bazaar district,

After hours of work, a tenn
porary telegraph wire was opened
between Quetta and Karachi
but was in operation less than
hour when it went dead.


Men Just Disappear


A special train bearing doctors,
nurses and medical supplies for
Quetta arrived there this after
noon.


While most of Quetta was de-
stroyed, some new buildings es-
capped, including the convent
school attended by the children of
many European families.


All nuns, priests and children in
the convent and adjoining church
at the time of the quake are safe.


The few minutes Of direct tele-
graph communication enabled the
first brief glimpSes of the disaster
to be seen. The telegraph master
reported four-fifthS of his staff had
disappeared" in the quake.


Six houses in the railway colony
collapsed instantly when the quake
struck, burying hapleSS families in
their ruins.


Sees Them Buried

home when he felt the first tremor.
arrived in time to see his wife and
children, who were just rushing
for the doorway, buried before his
eyes.

ficial and official world endur.
ance records, rested at the Key

ling ordeal which lasted q days,

ragged. The silver coat of paint
which once made the trim little
ship glisten with pride was
streaked, and reeking Of grimy oil
and grease.


The two brothers who pushed
the plane through rain and hail
stones for 653 hours Of continuous
flight, stuck close to their hotel
rooms though thousands waited
to congratulate them.


Throughout the night the two
brothers slept for a few hours and
were then aroused. This schedule
was followed for fear prolonged
sleep might have i'll effects upon
the two brothers who fought and
battled against fatigue to endur-
ance records far in excess Of all
previous marks.


Their flight to new endurance
laurels ended in a blaze of glory
for the two Mississippi youths
when late yesterday they brought
their plane to perfect three
point landing.


AS one, the $4,000 persons, who
filled the airport almost beyond
its capacity, gave one long and
lusty cheer as the "Ole Miss"
came to earth. A bare two minutes
earlier, as AL. who was at the
controls, jockeyed the plane into
position to land, they had gasped
in apprehension for the two be.
cause Of a flat tire on the landing
gear. But AL dipped the mono
planes nose and came in, steady
and to a perfect landing.


In remarkable condition, con-
Sidering the ordeal they had faced,
the two nevertheless presented
forlorn picture. The eyes of both
were swollen, and both were badly
In need of shaves and haircuts.

NEW YORK, December 28.-Radio
maestros sang the blues tonight as
they dourly contemplated the swan
song of their theme songs-and some
$4,000 other copyrighted tunes-at
midnight Tuesday.


Tin Pan Alley has been burning the
midnight oil in frantic efforts to bring
forth substitute themes to supplant
the musical trade marks which will be
withdrawn on and after January l
through the secession of eight music
publishing houses from radio royalty
contracts.


The houses are controlled by War
ner Brothers, which resigned this week
from the American Society of Com
posers, Authors and Publishers. This
body collects from the networks all
royalties from the tunes played over
the air and in turn pays the money
out to the publishers and individual
composers.


Royalty Called Inadequate.


The publishers, in resigning, said
the present royalty scale was tnsufh-
cient to compensate for sheet music
revenues lost through too-frequent
airing of the songs on the radio.


Unless the publishers can make in
dividual agreements with radio sta
tions-which appeared unlikely to-
day-the music Of some of Americas
foremost composers Of popular airs
will be banned from the airways.


In vain will radio listeners dial for
some of the music Of George Gersh-
win, Richard Rodgers, Jerome Kern,
Sigmund Romberg and other popular
composers. There will hardly be a
musical show left on Broadway whose
tunes may be broadcast. One of the
few major composers who will escape
radio exile is Irving Berlin, who pub
fishes his own works.

was bewildered over not being allowed

the publishing.


Paul Whiteman will have to get
along without George Gershwin's
Rhapsody In Blue" work which

waiting with bated breath for the

PEIPING, China, June % Sunday, 1,

ford, Mass, who was in the hands OF
Chinese bandits for seven weeks, was
turned over to American authorities

formation reaching the United States
legation here today.


Chinese rescuers reached the clergy

border, and then travelled to Canton
