ton was to the effect that Bush was
in good health, despite his period OF
captivity. Cantonese military author
tiles were given the credit for the
rescue.

Hhero of the occasion left hurriedly,
before they arrived. And he
didn't return.


But chilly souls gathered close
to the fire and gave silent thanks
for his act.

House early this morning.

MEXICO CITY, June G.N.S).
Four hundred persons persisted in
the lake district of Kochimiloo
when torrential rains inundated
the lowlands today. ,


The flood swept into crowded
parish church N the village OF San
Pedroactopan, drowning nearly
200 worshippers. The congrega-
ton was trapped when the roar
ing waters broke down the doors
and flooded the church.


Only seven of the 200 gathered
in the church for a religious tes'
tival escaped with their lives.


Eight Towns Flooded


In San Gregorio Atlapulco, the
wall of water swept down the main
thoroughfare carrying 20 persons
to their death.


Latest word said eight towns
were inundated, but an even
greater area may be affected.


A cloudburst which followed a
long period of heavy rain caused
the floods.


Fight Rescuers


Relief work was made difficult
by the superstition Of natives,
who attempted to bar rescuers
in the belief they were coming
to take away their churches.


The Mexican Red Cross and
the government participated in
immediate relief measures.


All of the villages affected lie
in a bowl formed by surrounding
mountains. The heavy rains
caused Kochimilco Lake to over
flow.


Muddy water ragged down
through ancient canals. filling
every village along them with
mud. San Pedroactopan was COW
cred with a layer several feet
deep.


When relief workers arrived,
indians of the villages were slosh-
ing about in the mud, crying their
ancient Aztec warning:


"Neche Maca MOma"-death
comes"


Some of the finest gardens on
the North American Continent
grew in this valley. Indians cul-
tivated flowers and vegetables of
unusual excellence, richly fed by
the fertile soil. These gardens all
were ruined.

Her head dropping. Anne Morrow

How much it was discolored and

heard, as Attorney General David T.
| Wilentz opened the prosecutions case
against Bruno Hauptmann.


Mrs Lindbergh listened bravely, her
face white and sad. She might. from
her expression, have been praying


In simple black dress with pink
touches black beret on her soft
hair-she sat just two chairs away
from Mrs. Anna Hauptmann, wife Of
the defendant.


Looks at Hauptmann.


Mrs Lindbergh today saw for the
first time the man accused of killing
her baby. Her eyes went repeatedly
to Bruno Richard Hauptmann's face.
No expression crossed her small oval
face, but her eyes we're tremendously
alive.


Betty Cow. the comely Scottish
nurse who put Charles A. Lindbergh.
jr., to bed the night he was kidnapped.
also looked occasionally toward the
man on trial for the death Of her
golden-haired charge.


Mrs. Lindbergh entered court quiet
ly, almost on tiptoe. Behind her en-
tered Miss Cow and Mrs. Ollie Wheat
ley, widow of the Lindbergh butler.
A lean-faced carpenter, who later
was accepted as juror, was being
| questioned when Mrs. Lindbergh ap-
peared. accompanied by Mrs. Norman
| SchWarzkopf.


Court Room Electrified.


Then an electric current swept the
courtroom, The ranks of spectators
murmured and half rose. Col. Lind
bergh looked at Anne anxiouSly, as she
crossed calmly in front Of Mrs. Haupt-
mann.


Her face was tranquil, and she
seemed a bit remote. She wore a
simple coat with a gray-brown fur
collar, which Mrs. Schwarzkopf helped
her lay aside.


The defendants wife Stunned the
! ordeal of a glance. She kept her head
averted, looking over the judges
bench


When Mrs. Lindbergh was seated.
her tall blond husband gave her a
reassuring smile, and they exchanged
long, straight look.


Then she looked straight ahead. 1t
was 10 minutes before Mrs. Schwarz-
kopf whispered. and Anne Lindbergh
glanced IN Hauptmann's direction, ap-
parently locating him for the first
| time.


Hauptmann's face was steadfastly
set in the direction of the witness
stand. If he was conscious Of Mrs.
Lindbergh's presence he gave no in
dication; but his wife, who had Sc
lected a chair where she could face
| him, became more nervous. Her head
| twitched and she shifted In her
chair.


Mrs. Whatley and Miss Cow, both
in brown, sat a row behind Mrs.
Lindbergh.

Tonsberg and Sandefjord, on Oslo
Fjord, are home ports for the great
whaling fleets that have pushed Nor
wegian industry far into Antarctic
waters. Eighty miles inland the ford
widens into an island-dotted lake on
whose northern shore is Oslo, set in
a curve of steep, wooded hills.


Save for an old church or two and
the thirteenth century fortress. Aker-
shus, that guards the harbor, there
Is little in modern Oslo to remind one
os the past. Among the principal
buildings are the royal palace, Stort-
ing CParliament) University and Ma
tional Theater, all reached by Karl
Johansgate. Rather curiously, this
main street of Norway's capital was
named for foreign ruler-Napoleon'S
general, Bernadette, who became
Charles XIV of Norway and Sweden.


On Bygdoy, a tree-covered island
west of Oslo, is the famous Norwegian
Folk Museum. Here, under open skies
or set in birch woods, are preserved
the homes of past centuries. Nor
ways wooden architecture, the prod
uct of her great forests, is character
istic of the country. Design, decora-
ton and even furniture are deter
mined by structure. In the low, dim
interiors, tables, benches and beds
are built into the rooms as solidly as
rafters and walls.


From December to April the snow
covered hills near Oslo are traced
with ski tracks and toboggan runs.
Korketrakkeren, alias Corkscrew Hill,
is best for tobogganing. On Sundays
and holidays, thousands pack the
trains for Holmenkollen, their skis
stacked in racks outside the cars. Two
cross country ski races are held dur
ing the Winter sports week that pre-
cedes Holmenkollen day. Contestants
in the jumping events must first quail
ify in these. One race is over a 10
mile course, the other covers ais
lance of 81 miles and is one of the
most difficult tests known to SkierS.


Oslos skating Kinks are worthy of
the city of Sonia Henfe, who has
held the world figure skating cham
pionship since 1927. International
skating competitions are another fea-
ture of sports week.


Nansen, who crossed Greenland on
skis, trained first on the hills about
Oslo. Amundsen, following the same
trails, developed the skill and endur-
ance that carried him to the South
Pole and back. At Frognersateren,
above Holmenkollen, is a ski museum,
with every known type Of ski, and
also relics of the great Norwegian
polar expeditions.


At Easter time, when the snow in
the lowlands has begun to melt, skiing
conditions in the mountains are per-
feet. Then Oslo declares a holiday
and young and old crowd the snow
trains bound north. Norway reaches
well above the Arctic Circle, and in
higher attitudes the skiing lasts
through May, despite frightening
days and hot Spring sunshine.

PEIPING, October 8.-Twenty-
eight missionaries, including IA
Americans, tomorrow are to begin a
hazardous 600-mile Yellow River fight
from Chinese Communists.


The American Embassy here was
advised the missionaries flight had
been precipitated as the Communists
began to move nearer to Lanchow in
Kansu Province from Szechuan.


The evacuating Christians are to
travel on RATS made of inflated goat
skins and face the dangers of bandit
attacks and river freeze-up. They
are heading for Paotow, a railhead,
where they will board a train for
Peiping.


The Chinese government has noti-
fed authorities along the tortuous
river route to afford every protection
to the fleeing group, which includes
some women and children.

HOLLAND, Mich, August 31.-Sen-
ator Arthur Il. Vandenberg, Republi-
can, Of Michigan, and Col. Frank
Knox. Chicago publisher. frequently
mentioned as Republican presiden-
tial possibilities, were under one roof
tonight. and the politically minded
were skeptical Of protestations that
the occasions was purely social.


That skepticism was enhanced by
the fact that. it was George F. Getz
of Chicago, treasurer of the Repub-
lican National Committee, who
brought them together at his Summer
home, near here.


There have been persistent rumors
that Col. Knox has lined up some
strong support. but Senator Vanden-
berg has discouraged the friends who
have offered quietly to attempt to
round up delegates for him.


Senator Vandenberg. who has been
resting at the Getz Summer home
since Congress adjourned, was host
at an informal party tonight. Getz,
Col. Knox and several prominent
Michigan Republicans were among
the guests.


The Senator denied that the gath
ering had political significance and
described his meeting with Col. Knox
as no more than a reunion Of two
personal friends and former Grand
Rapids (Mich.) newspaper men.


Michigan politicians had no hopes
that a formal announcement Of plans
would follow any conference held over
the week end. They did predict
however. that a definite understanding
between the two would be reached
before Col. Knox and Getz return to
Chicago.


Senator and Mrs. vandenberg ex-
pect to leave for a short European
tour in about 10 days.

able warriors armed with mortars,
machine guns and rifles.

Selassie Shuns Gas Use.

cent women and children must in
evitably be killed If its use were gen.
eral

ing itself and appealed to the EN-

Editor. McGill Commodity Service, Inc.


AUBURNDALE, Mass, April (41.
Commodity prices advanced during
the first week in April, now close to
the peak level reached in early March.
The advance was due to four groups,
namely, agricultural products, live
stock, hides and leather and nom
ferrous metals. During the week more
groups declined than advanced, as
seven individual groups-industrial
products. building materials, chemt-
Gals, fuels, paint materials, fine tex
tiles and vegetable oils-averaged less
than the previous week. In each
case, however, the reaction was OF q
limited character.


Industrial prices recorded slight
decline. Industrial activity held on q
relatively high plane during the first
quarter of the year and preliminary
figures for the first week in April show
only a moderate contraction.


Farm Prices Climb.


Agricultural prices climbed to the
highest level since February. The
continuance Of duststorms and sub
normal moisture have caused greater
speculative interest as there are signs
that 1885 will prove another year Of
crop deterioration. During the week
prices for wheat, corn, oats, rye, eggs,
sugar, f1axseed and butter averaged
higher. Four items declined-cotton,
wool, hay and beans.


Live stock, the third major group,
also moved upward rather sharply.
The latest index figure is 84.5, which
compares with 42.3 year ago. Price
strength in cattle and lambs more
than counteracted moderately lower
quotations for hogs.


The hide and leather index ad-
vanced due to a one-half cent mark
up In the price Of hides. Calfskins
weakened slightly.


Non ferrous metals reached a new
high for the year, rejecting higher
quotations for silver and tin. Anti
mony showed some disposition to de-
cline.


Fine textiles were weak, caused by
lower quotations for the two impor-
tant items-cotton and wool.


Vegetable Oils Decline.


Vegetable oils recorded the greatest
proportionate decline Of any Of the
seven groups that averaged lower as
compared with week ago. No items
advanced, while weakness occurred in

selves had 9 killed and so wounded.

Late yesterday afternoon one of
our detachments accommodating in the
TakkaZe sector repulsed an armed

1.-The adversary losses were serious

were killed, officers, Italian

Aviation has been most active

ended abruptly, with the soldiers in

aerial warfare and the. sailors at
home reported reliably to be getting
ready for action.

concentrations, menacing Gen. Ru-
dolfo Graziani's army at Dolo. In
the north they searched beyond the
Takkaze River for other enemy con-
centrations.

brief brushes by the ground forces
with the Ethiopian outposts.

lists, most of whom have served in
gun or powder rooms, were reported
called back to the service.


Informed sources concluded that
the navy was making ready for pos
sible eventualities, in the event that
the League Of Nations finally decided
to extend its arms, financial and
economic penalties against Italy to
include an oil embargo.


League discussion of a proposed oil
coal-iron-steel embargo was inter-
rupted by the advance of Franco-Brit-
ish peace proposals, but with the plan
for partition of Ethiopia discarded
by the League and repudiated by
Britain, Italian sources considered
q possibility that Anthony Eden, Brit
aims new foreign minister, might raise
the issue again.

H. Davis, the United States chief
delegate to the International Naval
Conference. told the Japanese today
that inasmuch as neither the United

of taking the offensive against the
other there is no reason to change
the existing relative power of their
two navies.


He made this statement to Admiral
Osami Nagano. the chief Japanese
delegate. directly across private con-
ference table.


Davis told the assembled conferees
that the usefulness of the Washing
ton treaty of 1922-which set the
British-American-Japanese navies on
a 5-5-3 ratio-had been fully DEM
onstrated, and that there was no rea-
son to change the existing system.


Nagano Stands Firm.


Admiral Nagano, however. did not
retreat single step from Japan's de-
mand for equality with the United
States and Great Britain in sea
power, declaring that Japan has made
great sacrifices in the Washington
treaty ratios.


He said these sacrifices would not
be repeated inasmuch as modern ships
and weapons had rendered Japan s
position more dangerous.
In informed quarters. it was stated
that the American-Japanese confer
ence could be regarded as resulting
in a draw.


After the meeting, the American
delegates went to the British admir-
atty to thresh out the details of the
Japanese plan with the British. The
British are standing Solidly with the
United States against the Japanese
demands for parity.


Compromise Proposed.

proposed compromised plan for feet

they would study the British pro-

definite understanding, however, that

should make a ''unilateral," or indi-
vidual, public declaration of its naval

mitments for more than one or two

WAIsENBURG, Colo, May 2.-The
dozen pupils in the lonely North Butte
school today mourned a friend they
never had met.


He was James G. Montijo, veteran
transport plane pilot, who was killed
when his plane crashed not far from
the school yesterday.


For months the children had
watched Montijo fly over on the Var
ney Co.'s route between Pueblo, Colo

his name and began writing to him.
He replied, and just before Easter he
new low over the school ground and
dropped basket of Easter eggs.


Yesterday they watched as he scared
over the school house circle, then
swerve and crash. Montijo was dead
when they reached the wreckage.


Nearby they found magazine. In
it was q letter addressed to the chill
dren of North Butte School. It ex-
pressed hope that the Easter eggs had
not been broken.


Montijo. who is credited with teach
ing Amelia Earhart to fly. Is Nlrvived
by his widow and tUo sons.

By the Associated Press.


AMARILLO, Tex, April ls.-Rain
brought Joy and renewed hope to the
southern edge Of the dust belt today.


Downpours and heavy showers
visited q wide area in the dust-torn
Texas Panhandle yesterday and last
night. benefiting the wheat crop and
grazing lands. in addition to bringing
relief from the blowing sand and silt.


The Oklahoma Panhandle, where
the residents have prayed for rain.
reported only clouds, however, and
the dust-stricken sections of Kansas,
Colorado and New Mexico still waited
for moisture.


Rain Brings Relief.


The precipitation near ChAdreSs,
Tex, amounted to about two inches
and at Quanah two inches of rain
fell in less than 80 minutes. A cloud
burst flooded cellars at Frederick. Till
man County, in Southwestern Okla
homa, and there were soaking rains
at other points in the State.


While the dust storms abated some
what over the rest of the stricken
sector, emergency hospitals we're
opened in Baca County, Colo, to care
for patients.


The school building at Walsh, Colo,
will be used to care for pneumonia
patients and the basement of a mortu-
airy at Springfield will be made avail
able chiefly for children suffering
from pneumonia and measles. An
outbreak Of the latter disease was
reported in the eastern part Of Baca
County.


Appeals for Aid Increase.


Heretofore patients have been taken
to Lamar, Colo. but increased appeals
for aid made necessary the establish
ment of hospital facilities nearer the
dust district.


Pneumonia. aggravated by dust, was
held responsible for the death of
Charles Williams, 68, at Springfield.

N. OAK, homes by dust storms, 125
persons passed through Livingston.
Mont, yesterday. Travelling in bat
tered motor cars, some loaded down
with home furnishings. the emigrants
hoped to find work and new homes in
Montana and Idaho.

SOFIA, Bulgaria, April 20.-Bul-
garia still had no cabinet tonight,
though Premier Designate Andrea
Toscheff had been comforting almost
continuously with military leaders dur
ing the last 36 hours.


Most of his time Toscheff, called
from retirement and botanical re-
search to help solve Bulgaria's govern
mental crisis, spent with leaders Of
the Military League, which is the
dominant factor in Bulgarian politics.


Although the league yesterday con-
sented to have the new government
consist of civilians, it apparently
feared return to the old system Of
political parties and declined to re-
linquish control of governmental af-
fairs until it was certain what form
the new government would take.


Another obstacle in Toscheff's way
was the many demands from civilians
slated for cabinet posts for the release
of former Premiers Kimon Gueorguieff
and Alexander Zankoff, whose arrest
and internment Thursday brought the
fall of the Zlateff government.

Editor. McGiu Commodity Service, Inc.


Commodity prices, which have
climbed with little interruption for
three years, now holding 86 per cent
above the extreme low, are not fac
ing materially higher levels in 1886.
In fact, only by artificial pressure or
unforeseen abnormal economic devel-
opmentS will prices escape consider
able irregularity and even weakness.


Business men are cognizant of the
terrific force of credit imitation but
the records of the past emphatically
indicate that credit initiation has a
more profound effect upon security
markets than it has upon commodity
prices. American business is organ
lied to operate under mass-production,
rapid-turnover and small-proflt-m
gin principles.


This will be true during the next
era of business activity above the
normal line. Meanwhile such power
ful forces as the law of supply and
demand, survival of the fittest, etc,
will prevent any runaway tendency
on the part of commodity prices to
reach higher levels.

AUBURNDALE, Mass, June % up.
Commodity prices again declined
during the third week of June. Con-

adverse Supreme Court decision de-

has been no collapse i'm the price
structure or any serious contraction in
industrial activity. Moreover, a sur
vey of the country shows that only
few attempts have been made to in
crease the number Of working hours

element of competition has increased
and as commodity markets are operat-
ing under natural economic laws, the
tendency Is for prices to weaken. The
composite index June 81 was 72.3,

during the third week of May of 74.4.

check-up shows that during the past
week only three groups averaged higher
and five declined. Six groups remain
unchanged.

Industrial prices have held stable
since the first Of the month. The
trend, however, has been downward
for several months. The latest index
Of 71.9 compares with 1913 at the turn
of the year and 1875 year ago. In
dustrial activity is now estimated at
"a per cent under normal.

sistance to bearish pressure. The in
dex for the week was slightly higher

NEW YORK, January 26.-The
stock market exhibited some nervous
ness today In the face Of renewed
weakness in leading foreign exchanges
and rather heavy tone displayed by
rail equities. Some amusement and
traction issues improved, along with
scattered specialties. The close was
irregular. Transfers approximated
100000 shares.


With the British pound dropping a
cent or more, and the principal Eu-
ropean gold currencies of several
points, most traders were not disposed
to extend commitments on the buying
side and there was some selling on
the theory that the week end might
bring bearish news.


Falling exchange rates were attrib-
uted partly to the fact that purchases
have diminished greatly due to the
uncertainty surrounding the gold
clause decision expected soon from
the Supreme Court. Fears have been
expressed that, should the ruling be
against the Government, the present
gold price might be substantially re-
duced. Thus buying of gold abroad
apparently will be at zero until the
high court hands down its judgment
and there will be little demand for
foreign moneys.


While the majority of stocks were
unable to resume their mild rally OF
the previous session, bonds were again
in demand. Carrier loans, despite the
softness Of rail shares, pointed higher.
Commodities, including grains and
cotton, were a bit easier in the early
dealings.

ferred got up 3 points, and Warner

Business and trade news generally

Miss Miley's Rally Tells.


MRS. ATWOOD defeated Marian
AA Leachman Of Vallejo, Calf, 2
and /, while Miss Miley vanquished
Margaret Russell, an outstanding
SHOEMAKER from Detroit, / up in
10 holes.


The Kentucky girl came from no
where to take her match. She was
four down at the turn and was still
two down with but three holes to
play. 1t was difficult position to be
in but she gritted her teeth and made
her shots stay even with par, to win
the sixteenth, tie the seventeenth and
win the eighteenth, and thereby finish
all even. On the eighteenth she got
down in two puts from 40 feet, while
Miss Russell needed three from 80 feet.


Miss Miley went boldly for the cup
in her 40-footer, knowing she had to
win the hole to stay in the play, and
her putt overran the hole dozen feet
Miss Russell left herself an eight
footer and missed it after Miss Miley
ran down her 12-foot shot.


Fine Chip Shot Decides Match.
ON THE nineteenth hole Miss Rus
sell was ahead on the drive and
brassie shots, and the match was de-
cided on the iron shots to the green.
The Kentuckian put hers just over the
green, while Miss Russell shot behind
a mound. The Detroiter's chip shot
then was short and she needed two
puts for a six, while Miss Miley
Clipped in two feet from the cup and
scored a five to win the match.


The match between Mrs. Atwood
and Miss Leachman was a see-saw
affair in the closing holes, with the
Chicagoan winning on the sixteenth
and seventeenth, the last with birdie
deuce.

PENNINGTON, N. j., January 25-
Despite near-zero weather at the trial
of Bruno Richard Hauptmann for the
kidnap murder of the Lindbergh baby,
Mrs. Hauptmann, hopeful and conf
dent, remarked that she didn't call
1t cold" Yesterday she seemed ner-
vouS, but not apprehensive as the
time of her husbands appearance on
the witness stand drew near He was
pale, but not visibly perturbed, save
for an occasional biting of his lower
lip but, according to all previous re-
ports, he has been eager to take the
witness stand.


Such vital and purely visual COM
municationS as Mrs. Hauptmann
flashed to him across the respondent,
but indomitable person of Lieut.. Smith
OF the New Jersey State police who
sits two seats from Hauptmann'S left,
and the bulky but less colorful Deputy
Sheriff Hovey Lowe.


But when the fateful words Bruno
Richard Hauptmann takes the stand, -
rang out in the court room. and the
telegraph messages flashed like a mad
flock of birds through the waiting
hands onto the wires, Mrs Haupt-
mann's composure was perfect.


Gaze Remains Steadfast.


Her face flushed, but her gaze did
not Waver. She watched. she listened,
perhaps she believed every word which
her husband uttered, but she showed
no notable sign of nervousness, simply
gazing at him with the mute faith of
woman to whom her husband is a
god.


Hauptmann walked to the witness
stand with the swinging stride of a
man who has never known the hideous
confinement of prison walls. He did
not swagger, he did not stink, he
simply stepped and then strode to
the chair which stands slightly above
his audience, and slightly below his
judge. He was neither manacIed nor
handled during this eventful progress
But Sheriff Lowe accompanied him
unostentatiously to his seat and sat
down directly behind him.


When Hauptmann was removed
@AOlAA NAAC oIoIlel Unexpectedly, Ills vile
seemed to relax and breathe more
freely, but when he came back, after
the testimony of the defense's first
witnesses, Mrs. Hauptmann was more
composed.


Apprehensive at Alibi Jolt.


After the little baker and his sharp
hard-faced assertive wife left the
stand, Mrs. Hauptmann turned a de-
voted and trusting gaze back toward
her husband. She had looked appre-
hensive as the Fredericksens failed to
convey any certainty in their answers
about that fateful March l, 1882. But
when Hauptmann took up his story,
she seemed reassured and once more
confident in the outcome.


Presently she shifted her attention
to the jury, watching, plainly trying
to read into their minds the same
confidence that has always been hers.


Her hands twisted nervouSly in and
out, her gaze shifted from her hus-
band to the jury and back, and now
and then to the judge and finally up
to the clock, as the afternoon dragged
toward an end and she felt the strain
that her husband must be feeling.


Her compoSure was excellent. None
could say that she, any more than the
carpenter himself, failed to present
complete containment in this ordeal.

BOSTON, Dec. 3.-Twenty.fivS
years ago Miss Anne Louise
Reinzi, master of seven languages,
barred her home to all comers.
One by one, gas, electricity and
water were turned off as meter
readers were refused admittance.


For the last quarter Of a cen
tury she spoke to no neighbor.
But last week the neighbors, who
despite constant rebuffs watched
over the 90-year-old recluse with
a kindly eye, noticed her absence
about the premises. They called
police who battered down doors
and found her lying on the floor
with a fractured leg. Yesterday,
still apparently a victim of the
delusion of persecution which the
neighbors said accounted for her
eccentricity, she died at City

TIFF1N, Ohio. June 1 tP).-A ter
rifle bomb explosion demolished the
front porch and badly damaged the
home of Charles E. Miller. president
Of Heidelberg College. early today.
Mr.. and Mrs. Miller and their
daughter, Gretchen. who were asleep
In the house at the time. escaped
injury. Every window in the house
was shattered. Windows in the sci
ence hall of the college a block away
and nearby residences were broken.


Police Chief Charles j. Mutchler
said that the bomb was made OF
dynamite. A burned fuse was found
under the front porch


Neither President Miller nor Chief
Mutchler could give any reason for
the bombing President Miller said he
had received no threatening letters
and had no enemies.


Heidelberg College was the scene of
student trouble in 1881. when college
students protested various social rules
which President Miller promulgated.
Dancing and other forms of student
entertainment were prohibited. Stu
dents circulated petitions TO college
authorities asking that the ban be
lifted on dancing and card parties, but
without success.


The students took the issue to the
Ohio Synod Of the Ohio Reformed
Church. which controls the college.
The Synod after heated debate over
ruled President Miller and permitted
dancing and card playing under GER
tain conditions.


Recently President Miller's garage
was painted during the night with
yellow stripes, but no one was ever
disciplined.


President Miller has been head of
the college for over 80 years.

VICE each week the country


hears about the President of the


United States meeting with the


members of his cabinet, but


only very few people have the
slightest idea of what cabinet session
is actually like.


Generally after each cabinet session,
there are hints and sometimes wild
speculation as to what was probably
discussed, but the real story never gets
out. Leaks are rare. Moreover, no
record is kept of these sessions.


AS matter of fact, these bi-weekly
gatherings around the long, highly
polished mahogany table in the cabinet
room of the executive office really are
nothing at all like what most people
imagine.


Quite naturally, the vast majority of
the people associate the cabinet with
silk hats cutaway coats, wing collars
and severe, thoughtful faces; faces that
never smile; voices that are cold and
commanding, and accustomed to whis-
pering. Few people would imagine
storytelling and laughter and joking as
being part of the makeup of cabinet
members when seated about the table
to discuss affairs of the world with the
Chief Executive.

She shook with fear. 1t was not fear
for herself 1t was fear for those
precious babies. Then she bounded
out of that thicket in plain view of

the ground. OF course the Dogs saw

for her. This was what she wanted.

catch her while she was fresh, not yet
tired with running. She would lead
gone only little way when she realized
that there was silence behind her.
With a perfectly fresh scent, easy to
follow, the voice of that Hound was
still What did it mean? They were
not following her. Had they gone
back?


Trembling, she waited with her great
ears set forward, straining to catch the
faintest sound to tell her where those
Dogs we're. For several minutes she
stood thus. Then, cautiously looking
and listening, she moved back along
her back trail. Presently she heard the
voice of the Hound He was back where
he had been when she showed herself
to him. With a sinking heart she
guessed what that meant. He was
picking up the old trail, the trail made

persisted in following that it would
lead him and his companions straight
to the thicket where those precious
babies were hidden. Mrs Lightfoot
dashed forward. Once more she
stamped her feet in sight of the Dogs

ginning if the Government intended
going to such lengths as deporting

AUBURNDALE. Mass, July 6 (P).-
Commodity prices during the week
ending July recorded considerable
stability with the composite price level
moderately higher than the last week
in June. The increase was due almost
entirely to price strength in the agri-
cultural group and particularly to fine
textiles which more than offset the
price weakness that was recorded in
the majority of groups. Out Of four
teen individual commodity claSsifica-
tions six declined during the past week
while only four advanced, and four
groups remain unchanged.


A check-up shows that since the ad-
verse Supreme Court decision out
of Is groups have registered a down.
ward trend Moreover. 8 out of IS
are holding well under the correspond
ing period year ago.


Farm Prices Hold Gains.


Agricultural products are primarily
responsible for the groups that are
higher than for the same period of
1884. For example. the agricultural
index, live stock, hides and leather,
coarse textiles and vegetable oils are
all higher than last year, whereas the
only industrial group that is holding
above year ago is non-ferrous metals.


Industrial prices advanced moder-
ately, movement that was due en-
tirely to fine textiles. Other indus
trial groups declined.


Agricultural prices also averaged
higher. The trend of individual groups
was mixed. Higher levels were noted
for wheat. eggs. butter and potatoes,
while corn, oats, rye and flaxseed
averaged lower.


Live stock, the third important
group, also moved upward during the
week as the price upswing in hogs
more than counteracted lower levels
for cattle and lambs.


Fuel prices were slightly lower, the
principal change being a reduction in
the price list of coke.


Paper and Pulp Sag.

fecting S5 per ton reduction in the
price list of newsboard.


Fine textiles represent the only
group that advanced outside of the
three major claSsifications-indu
and agricultural products and live
stock. Cotton was chiefly responsible
for the recovery. while raw silk was
slightly higher.

reaction being general. including CO.

NAPLES, Italy, August 24.-Thou-
sands of villagers fiocked into Naples
to cheer the embarkation for East
Africa today of nearly 5000 Black
shirts, including two sons OF Premier
Mussolini and son-in-law.


Wild enthusiasm marked the de-
parture of the steamships Saturnia
and Atlante Descriptions were broad
cast throughout the nation:


Mussolini's sons Vittorio and Bruno
and his son-i n-law, Count Galleazzo
Ciano, minister of propaganda, sailed
with aerial bombardment squadrons
All three had volunteered for active
service. G


II Duce himself was not. present
to bid them farewell, but his daugh-
ter Edda saw her husband, Count
Ciano, and her brothers off. Other
high Fascist officials were here to
wave farewell.


The big embarkation was ordered
as a part of gigantic effort by
Italy to finish sending the last con-
tingents of about 250,000 men to
East African colonies before the end
Of the month.


The waterfront was dark with eager
cheering humanity from early this
morning onward. The Atlante got
away first. bearing 1900 men and
officers. Hardly had the excitement
died down when the Saturnia, its
decks swarming with 4,700 soldiers
signaled its departure by blast OF
the siren.


The noise Of cheering men. Shrek
ing women and chanting Blackshirts
mingled with the whistled uproar of
all the ships in the harbor as the
big boat slowly drew away.

Awakened by the clink of thousands
of shovels removing one of the deepest
SHOWS since the Knickerbocker disaster,
in 1922, Washington struggled to work
late this morning in almost zero
weather over half-paralyzed street car
and bus systems


The rush hour found the thermom-
eter at the Winters minimum of six
above zero, a circumstance which
worked great hardship on street cars
equipped with underground ploWs.
Numbers of plows we're torn out in
slots contracted by the cold, and still
other street cars were derailed by ice
deposits.


The outlook in the wake of the IL
inch snow is for another night of in
tense cold, with a minimum of about
five degrees. The weather should re-
main fair, however, and after tomor-
row slowing rising temperatures are
expected through Saturday.


Thousands Clearing Snow.


Between 5,100 and 5000 emergency
relief workers began ShoVeling and
carting snow this morning, augment
ed by TOO regular District employees
The emergency workers will put in
six hours today and tomorrow, at 40
cents an hour, clearing streets, park
sidewalks, school yards, institutional
grounds and the Army and Navy air
fields.


Despite adverse conditions, the
street cars were kept moving slowly
into town. Thousands of StraphangerS
and hundreds of bus patrons were late
to work, and the city's large taxicab
feet proved wholly unequal to the
TuSh-hour demand.

feeder cable broke; and also at
Seventh street and Florida avenue and
Seventeenth street and Pennsylvania
avenue. There was tie-up at Con-
necticut avenue and Albemarle street
early this morning, and several hours
later two street cars were derailed on
the same line, one at Sedgwick street
and another at Davenport.

with less difficulty, but ran behind
schedule. Buses operating over Dis
trict streets, which had been cleared
by A snow ploWs yesterday and last
night, Jared better than those con-
meeting Washington with outlying dis
tricts.


Bus lines between Baltimore and
Washington and those operating in
many sections of nearby Maryland
and Virginia discontinued service yes
terday morning as storm conditions
made the roads too dangerous" for
traffic. The Maryland State Roads
Commission reported today, however,
that the highways would be put in
good shape" by noon.


Most of the secondary roads were
closed by drifts, with snow standing
on the level from to Is inches over
the State at large.

on heavy layer of ice was, with the
exception of 1112-inch fall on jan
uary 80, 1880. the deepest since 28
inches of snow sent the roof of the





theater audience during 1922.


Street-car and bus systems were
further taxed by additional thousands
Of motorists who usually drive to
work.


High drifts had marooned automo-

cold had frozen door locks in many

streets.


Record numbers of service calls
we're received by the American Auto

Automobile Club. Up until o'clock
last night the A. A. A. handled 1000
emergency calls, with every piece Of

crews of the other club also were kept

snow had seeped into door locks, and
motorists broke keys twisting them

locksmith in town was kept busy all
yesterday opening automobile DOORS

Harar regulars. started for the south
ern front today after being reviewed
by Ras Nasibu, who will command
them in battle against the Italians.

the soldiers rumbled southwark in
American-made motor trucks toward
the Fascist forces led by Gen. Rudolfo
Graziani.

a principal Ethiopian commander in
the south, told the Associated Press
that Jijigga, so miles to the east,
would be one of the main points of
defense on the southeastern front.


Reuters dispatches reported four
Italian planes attacked Gabradarre
today, dropping more than 200 bombs
and wounding seven Ethiopians.

Waterman.

sped back to town and summoned

met the officers with clubs and

wife at their home this morning and
then turned the gun on himself. Rela-
tives said Eye was crazed from drink
ing moonshine whisky.

nursed by Mrs. Eye narrowly escaped
being struck by the first charge from
the shotgun. Mrs. Eye fell on the
baby and only the quick action of
relatives saved the child from being
smothered.

ing heavily the past week and paced
the floor all last night. He previously
had been treated at a State hospital
for alcoholism. Relatives said they
knew no reason for his act except
drinking.


The couple is survived by four chill
dren, the eldest of whom is 8.

Adds ABABA, Oct. ga
comedy of diplomatic errors ended
today when the Italian minister,
Count Luigi Vinci-Gigliucci, and
his military attache, Captain Cal.
derini, were smuggled into a train
by Ethiopian authorities and
whisked out of Adds Ababa for
Djibouti so quickly that they were
unable to communicate with the
outside world.


Stay Gets Precedent


Count Vinci, whose strange
conduct in remaining here after
the Ethiopian government hand
ed him his passports and asked
him to leave created diplomatic
precedent, was taken early to-
day from the private home of
RaS DeSta Demtu where he had
been held virtual prisoner since
his refusal to get out of the
country.


He and his military attache
were taken swiftly to the sta
ton where they were kept under
heavy guard in the customs room
until the train was completely
beset by passengers.


A special coach with drawn
blinds, was stationed opposite the
customs room.


The train, made up further
down the station, was then backed
into the customs division, Count
Vinci and Calderini were rushed
aboard, and it steamed out so sud-
denly that those without tickets
who had been saying good-by
were forced to travel to the next
station.


Last Consul Out


On the train, but not with
Count Vinci, whose special coach
was guarded by IA soldiers and an
officer, were the German minister,
Hans Kirchholtes, and his wife,
bound on q weekend trip.


Count Vinci's departure, which
when heralded a fortnight ago,
created q worldwide sensation,
today awakened little local inter
est, nobody but journalists and
photographers possessing suffi-
cient interest to see him off.


The excuse for the long stay
by Count Vinci was that he de-
manded to await the arrival from
the interior Of the last Italian
consul.


The last one, from Megalo, ar
rived yesterday at Mojjo, where
Count Vinci's train will pick him
up today.

Washington's many public schools
had ceased today to be the bee hives OF
the past nine months, and the play
grounds of the city, busy only during
limited hours for that period, were
noisily active.


The reason, of course, is that yes
terday $4,000 children were dismissed
for the year.


In several schools, there were the
usual term-end ceremonies
tions, songs, drills and the like-but
in most of them, there were teachers
who remembered their own childhood
last days of school and just let the
ceremonies go.


School officially ended at pm. In
reality, by that time several thousand
children had been home or at play
for three hours.


Freedom for three months for the
children, however, doesn't mean the
same thing for all their teachers
Many hundreds of them will get a
brief respite from class room sLLervi-
sion only to become pupils again
Special teachers courses in many of
the leading colleges and universities
have attracted the largest number.
Others plan tours on which plaJ can
be combined with education 1isits to
Europe, Central and South America,
tours of the West, jaunts into Canada
and the North.


The teachers have another off,
cial days work 70 perform, too. When
they handed out the final report
cards for the year yesterday they
lacked some details in finishing the
formal clerical work of the year.

Europe.

Upon that, they said, may deter

system which France is attempting to
promote as well as Germany's future
attitude toward Frances program.

It may also decide. they said,

self marked out.

attack

condition as unsatisfactory"

sleep since Friday and had suffered
an overstrain of her nerves and heart

marshal's death. She was deeply shat

the marshal's close collaboration.


Government and opposition press

Annual reports of the collector of
internal revenue provide the effective
rejoinder to attacks by unfriendly men,
pers of Congress on the lump-sum
appropriation for the District. The ira
ditional form of such attacks is to treat
the lump sum as a gratuity wrung from
the hard-preSsed voting constituents
back home, and from this point to argue
for its reduction or elimination. Unin-
formed readers of the Record might form
the opinion that the people of the Dis
trict pay neither local nor Federal taxes.
but are supported as pampered wards
of the National Government.


AS a matter of fact, local residents
now pay about eighty-hve per cent of
National Capital maintenance and de-
yelopment expenses through their local
taxes. To the remaining fifteen per cent
they contribute heavily as national tax
payers. How heavily they contribute is
indicated by the report of the collector
of internal revenue for the fiscal year,
1885, just released. which shows the Dis
trict paid $12,638,14467 during that
period in internal revenue taxes-a little
more when processing taxes are included.


Comparison of the District payments
with similar payments made by the
States shows the District paying more
than any one of twenty-three States
Alabama, Arizona. Arkansas, Colorado,
Georgia, Idaho, Iowa, Kansas, Maine,
Mississippi, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada,
New Hampshire, New Mexico, North
Dakota, Oregon, South Carolina, South
Dakota, Utah, Vermont, West Virginia
and Wyoming.


The Districts payment exceeded the
combined payments of nine StateS-Ari-
iona, Idaho, Mississippi, Nevada. New
Mexico, North Dakota, South Dakota,
Vermont and wyoming. The Districts
payment was over fifteen times that of
North Dakota, twelve times that of New
Mexico. ten times of Idaho, nine times
each of Arizona, South Dakota and
Wyoming; eight times that Of Vermont,
six times that of Mississippi and Nevada;
four times that of Arkansas and Utah,
three times that of Montana and New
Hampshire, two and onehalf times that
of South Carolina, twice the payments
of Alabama, Maine and Oregon, one-half
greater than Nebraska and onefourth
greater than Kansas and West Virginia.


When the agricultural adjustment
taxes are included the comparison
shows only a slight change. In this
set-up the District ranks thirtyfirst
among the States, with the District pay
ment exceeding that of any one of
eighteen States. Here the payments of
the District exceeded by million and a
half the combined payments of seven
States.


The District is far more substantial
contributor to the lump sum, or other
Federal expenditures than are many Of
the States; matter which is emphasized
not in the spirit of slurring these States,
but in defense of the District against
malicious criticism as a tax dodger.
These States all have representation in
the Government which taxes them. The
taxpaying District has none.

BALTIMORE, September 21.-Ken-
dali Hill and Harry Jones. charged
with the staying Of Albert Atwell, Bal
timore cab driver, were brought to the
city jail here early today after threats
Of mob violence caused their removal
from Bel Air.


Four State troopers rushed the men
to safety here under close guard after
spiriting them away from the Hartford
County Jail. A crowd Of between so
and rs of Atwell's fellow drivers had
gathered in Bel Air after learning Of
their arrest.


Formally Charged.
Hill and Jones. both Of Perryville,
were formally charged with the slay-
ing Of the Baltimore taxi driver less
than eight hours after Atwell's body.
partly decomposed, was found in
clump of bushes near Havre de Grace
late yesterday.


The men were captured several miles
from Conowingo by a trio of State
troopers who overpowered Hill when,
they said, he attempted TO draw
pistol.


After several hours of questioning
at the Conowingo substation, officers
said, Jones admitted he and Hill held
up and robbed David Unger, another
cab driver, wednesday night, the day
after Atwell disappeared.
They denied, however, any connec-
| tion with the slaying
Man Was Strangled.
Magistrate ]. c. Vancherie of Havre
de Grace, acting coroner, asserted At
wells death was due to strangulation.
His hands had been tied behind his
back and pockets of his clothes looted
of their contents. {


Sheriff Granville C. Boyle of Har-
ford County said about rs taxi drivers
gathered in front of the Jail shortly
after midnight, and extra police were
ordered rushed there from nearby sub
stations.


State police, reconstructing the
crime, said they believed the men
hired Atwell's cab In Baltimore Tues
day night. robbed and killed him. and
dumped his body into the bushes. Both
men formerly were employed at the
Government Hospital at Perry Point.
! Magistrate Vancherie impaneled a
! jury last night to view the body. It's
verdict will be given September 80.

cALLANDER, Ontario, March
10 Q.N.SO More like a father
than a doctor was DR.. Allan Roy
Dafoe as he paid his daily visit
to the famous Dionne quontuplets
-Yvonne, Annette, Emile, Cecile
and Marie, born last May %.


The doctor put out his pipe as
he entered the spic and span
"Dafoe Hospital for the Quin-
tuplets" and, after disposing OF
some packages that were gifts for
the babies, donned white linen
Smock.


DR.. Dafoe stood there for min
ute peering through the glass win
dowS into the nursery room at the
babies-a short, heavy-set man
with an unusually large head and
close clipped, wiry gray hair, FUR
rowed face and twinkling eyes.


Recognize Doctor


There in the nursery were the
"uuints"-in their beds. Their
eyes lighted with recognition as
they saw the doctor. They kicked
and cavorted vigorously.


The babies room was bright and
colorful, with pink, yellow and
green blending harmoniously and
a flood of sunlight coming through
the large windows. Pink beds
with medals and tiny replica OF
Our Saviour on the cross pinned
to the top of each bed. CThe
quintuplets we're baptized Cath
olics.) Also in the room were five
little chairs with round holes in
the seats of each of them. Toys
were strewn about the room, with
in easy reach. Over in a corner
were five buggies. A closet nearby
was filled with towels and other
paraphernalia.


Babies Active


Entering the nursery room, DR..
Dafoe chucked Cecile under the
chin and said:


Hello, baby!"


Her eyes lit up and she caVorted
jubilantly on her tummy. She
pulled at the doctors spectacleS
and almost got them off.


Turning to another bed, he said:


'How are you, Annette?"


Little Annette tried to say it in
jumps. She pounded the bed with
her tiny fists.


From one to another the doctor
went. He laid the babies on their
backs, rubbed their tummies,
pulled their toes and chucked their
chins and made faces at them.
They all beamed.


First Tooth Arrives


There was quite bit Of excite
ment around the nursery because
two of the babies-Annette and
Yvonne-had cut their first tooth.
Annette was the first to show
signs of a tooth. You can imagine
the excitement! All Annette
could do was stare with her big
eyes as the nurses felt for that
tooth.


Each of the quintuplets was
rosy-cheeked from the air. They
have brown hair and large gray
brown eyes. Their big, round eyes
are their outstanding character
istic. Their bodies are we'll
formed and ruddy with health.


Three nurses in white, in
charge of the chief nurse, Mrs.
Louise De Keriline, a veteran in
Red Cross service, came in. They
wrapped the babies in pink
blankets and put pink knitted
bonnest on their heads. The
nursese wheeled in five brown
buggies with rubber tires, put
the babies in them and pushed
them out on the front porch
where. for three hours each day,
the quintuplets enjoy the fresh
air and sunlight.


Hospital Staff of Five


DR.. Dafoe later consulted Mrs.
De Keriline about the babies
weights, feeding and general con-
|dition.


Two Of the babies had gained
about two ounces, the other three
had lost about an ounce each.
But they were all getting
along fine. Yvonne, weighing is
pounds IL ounces, was the heav-
lest and Marie, weighing 13
pounds and 7A ounces, was the
highest. Their weights, however,
had been varying constantly.


The personnel of the hospital
consists of five persons, exclu-
Sive Of DR.. Dafoe. Mrs. De Keri-
line is in charge. The other two
nurses are Yvonne Lereaux and
''Pat" Mullin, the spare" nurse.
The houSekeeper is Laurence
Clusieux and the orderly is Tells
phore DemerS.

fore fire broke out she plunged
into the harbor.


Tugs rushing alongside attached
hawSers as the Seaplane began to

dashed safely.

aged, both floats were torn away
and it was believed the hull was
also damaged.

many's Do-X was retired, had gone
through only a part of her tests
when she was flown up from Bor'
deaxu to greet the liner Nor
mandie.

MEMEL, September 30.-A crowd
of puzzled, irritable voters gathered
today at polling stations under heavy
police guard for the second day OF the
election between German and Lithu-
anian candidates for the Memel ter
rttory's Diet.


The extension of the elections fol-
lowed a breakdown Of the arrange
ments yesterday. when the compli-
Gated voting procedure prevented an
estimated 40 per cent of the populace
from casting ballots.


The police re-enforcements resulted
from yesterdays rioting at Juknaiciai,
near the German frontier, where three
policemen were beaten severely.


Election Urns Smashed.


The entire balloting, it was reported
reliably, will be repeated at Juknaiciai,
where voters. exasperated by the de-
lay, smashed election urnS, wrecked
the polling station and attacked
members of the Election Committee.
Indignant crowds besieged the dis
trict's 76 polling stations until late
last night, demanding the right to
vote Immediately. Due to the COM
plicated system, the earliest returns
were not expected before Friday.


The hitch which led the Lithu-
anian cabinet to amend the election
law and extend polling into the sec
ond day arose from delay by citizens
in choosing their candidates for 29
seats in the Landtag.


Voters were instructed to tear of
% sheets, bearing the names of can
didates for as many Diet seats from
book holding the names Of more
than 100 aspirants to the Diet.


Election authorities had estimated
the task could be done in 10 minutes,
but many of the citizens insisted on
taking half hour or more.


Bitterness Stirred.


The extension Of the polling into the
second day stirred bitterness among
both Memellanders and Germans who
seek to restore East Prussia's Oldest
city, lost by Germany in the World
War, to Nazldom.


In addition to the clash at Juknai-
ciai, there was disturbance at the
village of Prokuls, where men posting
election signs were attacked, some
shots were fired and four persons were
injured.

The Civil Service Commission yes
terday sent out to Government estab-
lishments instructions for applying
the new efficiency rating system which
gets its initial try-out when the an
nual ratings are made May IS.


The new system does away with
the fine numerical distinctions of
the old.


In sending out the instructions,
the commission said:


THE present plan of recording the
efficiency of employees, like any other
plan having the same purpose, re-
quires intelligent action, considered
Judgment and mutual cooperation
on the part of rating officers, re-
viewing officers and boards of review.
The plan affords a convenient uni
form vehicle for recording these judg-
ments, but the usefulness of the plan
and the value of the efficiency ratings
when made depend upon the degree
to which all the rating officials CO.
operate before, during and after the
rating process in acquiring and ap-
plying a correct understanding Of the
rating tasks and responsibility and a
common understanding of rating
standings and the terms in which
these standards are expressed.


Under the new rating scheme, en-
ployes are graded excellent, very good,
good, fair and unsatisfactory. When
employees have a rating of excellent,
very good or good they are eligible
for pay increases. When unsatisfac-
tory they are not to be continued
longer in the work upon which en-
gagged, but assigned to duties more
nearly commensurate with their abil-
ity. The new efficiency rating scale
was devised after lengthy study
by personnel officers throughout the
Government in cooperation with the
Civil Service Commission"

former countess as fortune hunting

riage was only step in the con-
spiracy."

Mrs. Ryan returned her husbands ex-
pensive gifts to the jewellers and with
the credit obtained bought. wrist
watch for Mittrovsky and had it en-
graved in German:


II am with you every hour"

ruary 20, 1894, the Ryan's wedding
day.

rious false pretenses, denied herself to

mer countess continued to commune
cate with Mittrovsky after her mar
riage and assured him that she was
marrying the plaintiff only for Count
Mittrovsky." The Ryans separated
less than three months after their
marriage.

lionaire dies and the "ex-con" re-
forms and takes over the estate

A MAN who had been away from
"A his home village for IA years
visited the old Sunday school, and
was able to tell the names Of all the
new members who were not there IA
years previously, because he could
see the resemblance of the children
to one or the other of their parents.


While no two persons are exactly
alike in face or body, nevertheless
certain characteristics Of face and
BODY are handed down to children.
In speaking of the different types, DR..
Llewellys F. Barker, Johns Hopkins
University, speaks of four different
groups:


l. Those of the pyknic (cycloid)
type (called the bulldog type by
some of us) are short, round and
stubby. In disposition they are "hail
fellow well met"-booSters, backSlap-
pers. They are predisposed to mental
depression states, diabetes, rheuma-
tism. arthritis, apoplexy and high
blood pressure.


2. Those of the asthenic type (the
greyhound type) are tall, slender, re-
served, looking inward with their
thoughts, and are predisposed to de-
mentia precoX, a persistent dream
state, tuberculosis, ptosis, dropping
downward of the stomach and other
abdominal organs and low blood pres
sure.


3. The athletic type, between the
first two with the tendency to de-
mentia precox-day dreaming


The dyplastic type includes the
giants and dwarfs, when the ductless
glands are probably at fault.


In a magazine article I wrote some
years ago, Does Your Shape Affect
Your Health" 1t was pointed out that
the person with the long body and
short legs would be strong physically,
but might easily overeat and suffer
with diabetes, heart failure and high
blood pressure. The slender person,
with long legs and short body, might
easily suffer with tuberculosis and
indigestion, as the narrow body gives
insufficient room for the lungs and
stomach; the small intestine is often
shorter than normal. which means
less surface for the blood to absorb
nourishment from food.


Now, the fact that you have long
body and short legs doesn't mean
that you are bound to have heart, kid
ney or blood-pressure ailments. Nor
does the fact that you are slender
mean that you will have tuberculosis
indigestion and low blood pressure.


1t simply means that there will be
tendencies toward these ailments, so
whatever your shape, you can protect
yourself by knowing this.

LONDON, July 20 P).-The British
cabinet today moved to formulate a
definite decision regarding the ma
tons policy at the forthcoming
League of Nations Council on the
Ethiopian dispute.

this purpose, authoritative sources
stated today, has been tentatively set
for next week.


The necessity for such a clearly
defined policy became apparent with
the denial in authoritative quarters
that Great Britain favored an Italian
protectorate over Ethiopia.


Reports had persisted that Anglo
French diplomatic exchanges had
dealt with such protectorate.


The League itself would not coun-
tenance that arrangement, it was
pointed out, as both Italy and Ethiopia
are members of the League.


Pending the meeting of the cabinet,
Sir Eric Drummond, British ambas-
sador to Rome, is pursuing efforts to
persuade Premier Mussolini to Join
the League discussions.


Parliament will discuss the Italo-
Ethiopian question Tuesday.

plause after another for the blue
clad middies from the time that they
arrived at the station for their first
invasion of New Haven until they left

took kindly also to Navy mascot-a

middies pieced together several pic
lures, among them that of bucking

topped of their pictorial gymnastics

fast there to the Yale campus, and
later from the campus to the bowl.

the village which the buccaneers
raided yesterday, taking of every child
in school.

save 10 children, but they killed four
of the pirates and captured three.
One o. the three pirate craft was
sunk, but the other two, carrying 20
children, fled. One child was killed

rewed their supplies and ammunition

the junks.

lage and quickly overpowered the 10

ing the town the outlaws raided the

A disagreement between Secretary
Perkins and the House Ways and
Means Committee over social security
machinery remained unsettled today.


1t had reached the point where one
Democratic leader suggested Miss
Perkins should be barred from final
conference the committee will have
with President Roosevelt before pre-
senting the bill to the House


The major points of the dispute are
two: Miss Perkins says the Social In
urance Board, which will handle much
Of the social security plan, should be
under her Department of Labor: the
committee has voted to make the
board independent. The Labor Sec
retary contends all employers with
four or more workers should be sub
ject to the unemployment insurance
tax; the committee, over her protest
raised the figure to 10 workers.


Committee Adamant.


Though the committees hearings
ended three weeks ago, it was learned
today that Miss Perkins has continued
informal discussions with committee
members. attempting to get them to
change their minds. They have been
adamant.


Once she asked that the differences
be discussed in a special meeting with
the President. but informed sources
on Capitol Hill said the President de-
clined to grant q conference until the
final draft of the bill was ready for
his inspection.


One high Democratic leader. who
asked that his name be withheld be-
cause he could not afford to pick a
public fight with a Democratic cab
met member" said one reason the
committee had been slow in report
ing the bill to the House was Miss
Perkins interference"


Seeks Separate Conference.


He said he had suggested to Chair
man Doughton that when the COM
mittee makes its final trip TO the
White House, it insist that none other
than committee members and the
President be present.


Il told him that if Miss Perkins
was present, she would run the con-
ference-take charge of things" the
leader said. The committee should ask
the President to have his conference
with Miss Perkins at some other time :"


Miss Perkins had some of the Dem
ocratic committee leaders as her din
Ter guests recently. But outside of
few smiling remarks about how the
social security bill had been side
tracked, the guests said that measure
was not discussed

A volley of pistol fire killed one young

hospital.

TOXIC, June 29.-The worst rain
storms and floods in half a century
deluged the populous and thriving
Osaka, Kyoto and Kobe Districts to-
day, the second time in less than 10
months that the industrial heart Of
the Japanese empire has been para
lyzed by a natural calamity.


Sixty-two persons thus far were
known definitely to have perished,
but many were still missing and
scores were injured.


Thousands were driven from their
homes and fragmentary survey OF
the affected area indicated that at
least 10000 houses and buildings
we're inundated. Damage was esti-
mated at more than 100000 yen
(about 2,sooooo).


Flood Hits Typhoon Area


The floods also swept over North
ern Kyushu and Shikoku Projects
and Western Hondo, the same regions
scourged by a disastrous typnoon
September %. 1884.


Crews of go fishing boats were
missing off Keishohokudo, Province
of Korea. Rescue vessels set out to
search for them.


Floods also swept Southeastern
Korea following torrential rains Fri
day.


Communications were disrupted
and railways were washed away IN
MANY sections. Serious damage to
crops was feared.


The Prefectures Of Fukuoka, Naga-
saki and Yamaguchi bore the brunt
of the floods, where damage was IN
creased by heavy winds.


Kyoto Suffers Worst.


Kyoto, lying in a valley encircled
by mountains, suffered the worst.
Rivers, a picturesque feature OF the
ancient capital of Japan, surged over
their banks and became torrents OF
destruction. They washed away 81
bridges.


The city's transit systems were dis
rupted and the waters compelleo
thousands to take refuge In Buddhist
temples crowning the hills about the
city. =,


One estimate was that 10000 dwell
ings in Kioto alone were flooded, while
Fushimi, suburb Of Kioto, had scores
of houses submerged to their caves.


Army engineers were called out ootn
in Kioto and Osaka to attempt to curb
the ravages of the food and other
troops were assigned to rescue and
police duties.


Early reports indicated the movie
center in Kioto, Japan's Hollywood,
suffered heavily. The steel center In
North Kyushu, a leading factor in
the empires booming munitions in
dustry, also suffered heavily.


Iron Works Closed Down.


The great Yawata Iron Works was
compelled to close down, with an esti-
mated loss Of half a million yen Tor
each idle day.


Water mains burst at Kobe and a
drinking water shortage was threat
ened. All schools in the stricken area
were closed.


Late today traffic was restored on
the Tokaido Railway, the empire $
main trunk line. linking Osaka and
Toxic, but suburban traffic in K1oto,
Osaka and Kobe was still disrupted.
Telegraph and telephone lines were
down over wide areas.


The storm was reported moving
northward from Osaka, but 1t was
believed Toxic would escape it. No
Americans were believed to have been
involved in the disaster.

BY the Associated Press.


FLEMINGTON, N. j., February a.
Mrs. Anna Hauptmann found con-
ISOLATION today in Attorney Lloyd
Fishers words, ''Well see this thing
through"


Fisher, a member on her husbands
legal staff, spoke to her after the
jury,s verdict finding Bruno Richard
Hauptmann guilty of killing the Lind
bergh baby.


Tears rolled down her cheeks for
the first time since the trial began
January 2.


Fisher, who has been her husbands
chief confidant, came to her side
and said:


Now you be brave. Don't show any
emotion here. Don't show anything.
Well see this thing through"


Wife Stin Has Hope.


Mrs. Hauptmann's chin was quiver-
ing, but she frightened her pale lips
and left the court room saying:


II still hope and I'm not afraid"


After six weeks, 1t was all over in
81 minutes. During the first part of
the grim proceeding. Mrs. Hauptmann
seemed not to grasp what had hap
pened. She heard gray-haired
Charles Walton, ST., the jury fore
man, report the verdict and heard
the jury polled without moving.


Her expression did not change until
Hauptmann looked at her, closed his
eyes and slowly shook his head.


Tears came then in her dull blue
eyes, but did not fall until Justice
Trenchard began the sentence.


Weeps as Jury Leaves.


When the crowd began to leave and
the jury filed out she looked at the
farmers, laborers and housewives who
had voted Guilty of murder in the
first degree" and began to weep anew.


Earlier in the trial the plain look
ing former waitress said. Few women
know what it is to love their hus-
bands"


On the eve of the verdict she said ::


Il keep thinking we'll be back
together. I've done everything
could. I can't think of anything else
I could have done.


He told me he did wrong in the
old country, but I forgave him and
we started all over again. When this
is through we'll start over again"


After the verdict she said, Life
holds nothing for me-"

by the huge thrush Of water to the

millions. The larger vessels anchored
in the harbor suffered relatively slight
damage.


The liner Conte Di Savoia was torn
from its moorings and swept down the
harbor. The vessel was saved from
crashing into wall and other nearby
boats by tugs.


Two other vessels, the Sierra Ven
tana, recently acquired for military
transportation purposes, and tanker

back to the dock undamaged.


The San Giorgio pier, at which

CHICAGO, March e.-Men's ap-
parel merchants experienced a fair
turnover and lower costs and came out
of 1884 with net profit, the sixth
annual Nationwide business survey
made by the National Association of
Retail Clothiers and Furnishers shows.


Summary of the recently completed
survey indicated profits were created
in 1884 on a different basis than in
1888, one of several unusual circum-
stances in the trend of clothier's busi-
ness.


The margin Of net profit among
smaller stores, the survey revealed,
was Just a shade better than a year
ago-36 per cent, as against 81.
Among larger stores, it jumped from 2
per cent to So per cent. The survey
showed big volume clothiers had the
edge because of more efficient mer-
chandising. Their profits were higher
even though expenses were greater.


Pointing out that salary and other
expense items declined substantially,
the survey indicated small stores could
hardly blame the retail code for their
less desirable showing. On the other
hand, said the National Clothier, trade
journal of the association, raising
prices-forcing the merchant to cut
his mark-up-would be circumstance
confronting large and small stores
alike, and "the larger firms were ap-
parently unharmed by it to any great
extent"


Other highlights of the survey we're:


Advertising costs for small stores
increased: for large stores it was less
than for the previous year.


Busheling expense was less for the
small stores; greater for the large ones.


Taxes were lower for the small
group; higher for the large group.


Accounts receivable charged of we're
slightly lower for the small stores;
slightly higher for the large ones.

BUTTE, Mont, December 27.-Butte
police announced today the body Of
Floyd Woods, A., ranch caretaker, be-
lieved to have been the fourth victim
of William Henry Knight, ex-convict,
had been found.


Posses securing wide area in the
hunt for knight throughout South
western Montana reported to police
headquarters here this morning that
the body Of Woods was located on a
sand bank on the Madison River near
Ennis, about 80 miles southwest Of
here.


Woods had been shot to death.


Discovery of Woods blood-stained
automobile, led officers to the con-
clusion he was slain by Knight, for
abandoned near Woods garage was
the motor car in which Knight fed
from Butte after Christmas shooting
affray.

Walsh were killed and Policeman
James Mooney and Mrs. Florence
Benevue were wounded. Mooney said
Knight was the killer.

bloody trail led from his garage to the
road. Car tracks we're followed to a
bridge over Madison River, where
more bloodstains were found, leaving
police to the belief Woods body was
tossed into the stream.


When Woods car later was found
abandoned near Anaconda, nearly 200
miles from his garage, officers concen-
trated their search in that area.


Jean Miller, sister Of Mrs. Benevue
and former companion Of Knight,
gave information leading Sheriff w.
B. Severyns Of Seattle to name Knight
as the slayer Of Deputy Sheriff Thomas
Meehan, killed near Seattle Novem-
Der 13.


Police Chief Walter Shay said the
woman, held on a technical charge,

"squeal" when he started the Butte
affray.

Charges that the Coast Guard cut

rum ship, Casanova, in neutral waters

Zoole of the American ship.


The commanders written report to
Coast Guard headquarters said the
Casanova was only 13 miles OF Block
Island, r. l., December % when first
sighted and that its speed was Judged
to exceed 13 knots"


Under the treaty with Great Brit
ain, rum runners are permitted no
nearer than "one-hour's sailing" time
from the American coast.


Capt. Bennett of st. Johns. master
of the Casanova, averred that his
craft was lying at anchor 20 miles
off Block Island when the cutter
came upon her.


Comdr. Zoole reported six shots
were fired in the chase, three of them
blanks. The Casanova halted. but
zoole was instructed by his superiors
to release the vessel.

ABOARD THE S. S. HOUSTON.
October 19. - President Roosevelt
pulled out into the Atlantic TODAY from
the San Bias Islands for Saturday
fishing before pointing the Houston
northward for home this evening.


The tropic sun has baked the faces
OF the President and his party. but
all hands aboard are eager for another
try at their luck in deep sea fishing.


The President today was delighted
over the events of yesterdays visit to
the San Bias Indians In their
matched huts on the thickly populated
Islands. He and his party are carry
ing home number of souvenirs pur-
chased from the shy. brightly dressed
women. who covered their faces to
cameras.


Heads Home Tonight.


Tonight the President will reboard
the Houston, which will head north
Tor Windward Passage, between Cuba
and Haiti. The destination Is be-
heved to be Charleston. S. c., about
the middle Of next week.


When the President and his fellow
adventures neared shore in several
OF the ships boats yesterday they were
met by smiling, brown native bows.
who skillfully padded their dueouts
10 form a guiding convoy back TO the
beach.


Receives Chief.


The chief wore an old infantry
campaign hat with regal pride. His
clean old flannel shirt hung outside
his soiled trousers Horn-rimmed dark
glasses protected his eyes from the
sun. He proudly bore away the ciga.
rettes the President had given him
when they exchanged presents in ira
ditional courtesy His gift to the Pres.
ident consisted of shark teeth and
spears. Friendliness prevailed on all
sides.


The huge police dog accompanying
Capt. LIE Breton of the Portland Gre
ated excitement among the crowds of
natives who emerged from their
closely built huts among the cocoanut
trees wherever the party wandered.


Hundreds of boys and girls trooped
after the dog and gleefully called his
name-"Offy.2

TN THE noble Hall Of the Americas


at the Pan-American Union where


the United States service bands
u so often have played the music OF
Latin America, there gathered last
evening the most picturesque group OF
musicians that ever has visited the
Capital The OrQuesta Tipica de
Policia de Mexico, under the direction
Of Maestro Miguel Lerdo de Tejada, an
organization of 10 men, brought Joy to
the hearts of their countrymen and
stirred the blood Of their American
neiRhbors in one Of the most colorful
concerts presented in that beautiful
auditorium.


The trim uniforms Of the service
bands were replaced by rich Mexican
costumes, elaborately embroidered and
the huge sombreros adorned with sill
yer so much more romantic than the
conventional headgear of the general
public. There was a riot Of color
everywhere, In the scarfs knotted
about the throats of the players, in
the "SarapeS" thrown carelessly over
the shoulder and in the draperies
scattered about amongst the inStru-
ments. Against this background sat
the musicians, dark of visage with
mobile features and flashing eyes.
Across their knees lay the guitars and
saltarios, native instruments whose
tonal color was to merge with the
marimba, the violin, the double BASES
and the horns that form the ensemble.


Playing Effective.


The musicians waited with that
patience and immobility only acquired
in land of sunshine until the arrival
OF suave and elegant Maestro de Tejada
announced the beginning of the con-
cert. With lift Of the eyebrows and
slight but telling indications of his
graceful hands he led his men into
the stirring strains of his own compo-
sition, Marcia Patriotica." With the
opening measures there arose rich,
melodious sound, harmony and rhythm
combined, in which no instrumental
medium was discernable, but which
became music of the most effective
kind.


The men of the orchestra played
without the printed page before them,
but with their eyes fixed on their con-
ductor. No mere setting down of notes
were needed, for they played from
their hearts and with their entire
being. The old man with the huge
guitar and the skilful and fleet players
Of the saltario surely had little use for
musical script, for this was the music
they had known from infancy and
played at every fiesta or in the twilight
hours when the days work was done.
Incredibly swift in their movement
over the strings and united as one
man in their feeling for effects, they
threw themselves into the swing of
the music with complete abandon.


And the effects that we're produced:
Here beautiful purring pianissimo, a
melodious whisper from somewhere
and then a rising crescendo that grew
in might and volume with uniform
exactness and infinite understanding
of spacing into glorious quantity Of
sound that held Secreted the mechani-
cal means by which it was achieved.
This was music Not the kind that
came from studied violin tone and
matching Of cello or woodwinds, but
music of the universe, grand and noble
and heart touching.

QUANTICO. Va, May CP).-The
waters Of his native State smacked
against his f1agship's bow today as
Rear Admiral Richard E. Byrd re-
turned home from his second Ant
arctic expedition to receive a hero's
welcome.


Passing through the Virginia Capes
as the first white settlers in the New
World had done more than 800 years
ago, the adventurer aboard his flagship
Jacob Rupert set course that would
carry him first to the Marine base at
Quantico and then to Washington for
President Roosevelt's greetings and
congratulations.


The supply ship Bear of Oakland
was the first through the Capes. with
the Rupert following last night. At
Quantico the expeditions leader plan
ned to leave his flagship, which could
not negotiate the shallow water of the
winding Potomac, and proceed to
Washington aboard the Bear Of Oak
land.


Whistles screamed when the Jacob
Rupert, trailing seven hours behind
the Bear of Oakland, dropped anchor
in Hampton Roads last night.

averaged less than 4 per cent. These
levels were not reached again until
the two years which preceded Ameri-
cas- entrance into the World War and
the 3.45 per cent rate, average of those
years, remained the low point for the
first 80 years Of the century. accord
ing to the Alexander Hamilton In
stitute.


The rate to which the money market
has become accustomed since 1880,
however, are so low that the bottom
of the first 80 years seems extremely
high in comparison. While business
improvement has been in evidence
since the middle of 1882, the irregu-
lar but sustained recovery has been
accompanied by declining commercial
paper rates. The movement has been
without evidence of strain in the short
term money market.


The supply of loanable funds coupled
with the exceedingly slack demand
which has been in evidence thus far
during the recovery suggests that a
business expansion may progress con-
Siderably further without material
change in the money market rates.
The import is that, so far as the money
market is concerned, not only are con-
ditions favorable to further business
expansion but the conditions which
threaten an expansion from this source
appear remote.

NEW YORK. November 9.-The
National Automobile Show closed its
thirty-siXth annual run tonight and
Alfred Reeves, manager. promptly
labeled it the largest retail selling
show since 1929"


Some companies have almost
doubled their sales, with the average
more than 60 per cent above those for
the show last January" said Reeves,
vice president and general manager
of the Automobile Manufacturers As
sociation.


Exhibitors generally praised the
plan of holding the show in November
instead of January.

usually bright outlook" for 1886 in
both the domestic and export markets


Forty-two motor car dealers from
Germany arrived in time to attend the
final day. They plan TO leave Monday
on tour of factories in Detroit, Flint
and other cities.

will be dismantled and shipped to
shows in other cities. Most of them
will cross the East River to Brooklyn,
where display will be held next
week.

Central Palace, opened last Saturday.

NEW YORK, Dec. 6 U.N.S0.
The North German Lloyd liner
Bremen, escorted by an armed
convoy of five vessels through New
York harbor, docked without Incl.
dent today despite advance warn
ingS of Communist bomb plot.


A force of so police. augmented
by IS special officers. turned the
pier into a fortress aS the giant
liner was warped into her berth.
There were 627 passengers, includ-
ing 281 Americans, aboard.


Three police launches and two
coast guard vessels conveyed the
Bremen up the harbor.


Tips that Communists planned
to blow up the Bremen in the
harbor were believed based on
statements attributed to Louis
Weickum, publicity representative
for the line, that a mysterious air
plane cruised over the Europa,
sister ship of the Bremen, and ap.
parently fired several shots near
quarantine several weeks, ago.


Commodore Leopold ziegenbeim
of the Bremen profesSed ignorance
of the bombing scare, although he
recalled that Communist riots
aboard the vessel last July delayed
her sailing for several hours.


The suspicious actions of two
young men who attempted to leave
the Brennan caused customs autho-
rites to detain them for question
ing today after the ship docked.
Claiming to be German subjects,
they explained they had not been
passengers, but had boarded her
after she docked. They were seized
as they attempted to leave the
gangplank because they had no
landing cards.

ers, and said that, despite their cam
