Many gardeners make tne mis-.
take of applying fertilizers too
early and too freely. Trees,
shrubs and rosebushes need no
artificial feeding at planting time.
They will find all the plant food
they need in the soil until new
root growth has been made and
new top growth started. There
is always danger that CONNER
cial fertilizers will damage the
few roots that remain on plants
just set out. Later plant food in
abundance will be needed. Estab-
lished plants, trees and shrubs,
and particularly lawns, can be
fed now to great advantage. A
balanced fertilizer from the seed
stores or one Of the prepared
fertilizers now on the market Is
best for the amateur, who should
remember that most plants need
something besides bone meal,
which, after all, Is q very slow
acting fertilizer and not to be
recommended for quick results.

MERIDIAN, Miss, June 90
Weathering tempest and overcoming
fire, AL and Fred Key, the long-dis-
tance Meridian flyers, today winged
their way past 600 hours of sustained
endurance flight.


The recognized official world record
was passed Thursday afternoon at
1880 pm. Central standard time on
their twenty-third day of continuous
flight over and around the Meridian
Airport and a new world record was
set an hour later.


Unsatisfied by Record.


But a new world record did not
satisfy the intrepid flyers, and the
brothers zoomed on in their attempt
to surpass the 647-hour flight of Dale
jackson and Forest O'Brine, which
was not officially recognized because
of an improper Paragraph.


The brothers asserted the endur-
ance plane, Ole Miss, was still per-
forming smoothly.


AL and Fred entered their 600th
hour of flight at 1882 pm. today
after they had run safely through a
night storm and had fought off a
morning fire in the planes battery.


Today, just after a refueling con-
tact. the planes battery burst into
flames, but AL Key, at the controls,
quickly shut off the ignition, pulled
down fire extinguisher and put out
the blaze. The plane dropped to
within 200 feet of the airport before
he gave her the gun again.


Must Make Satisfactory Landing.


For the Keys to claim the world
record they have set they must make
a satisfactory landing on the munich
pal airport, now called Key Field
from which they took off on June f.


The flyers we're buoyed in their
continued fight by $100-a-day
bonus for every day they remain aloft
over and above the world record, and
they have not yet announced any
immediate intention of coming down.

By the Associated Press.


LA SALE. ILL.,, January l6.-Five
terrorist bank robbers, who killed a
bank cashier and the sheriff of
Marshall County, wounded two others
seriously and kidnapped l3-year -old
farm boy whose automobile they had
stolen, were surrounded by the police
in a field near Varna, Ill.,. today
Three of them were reported wounded


The dead we're Glenn Axline, sheriff
of Marshall County, and Charles
Bundy. cashier of the Leonore State
Bank.


The wounded were Charles Feipp,
member of the Board of Super
visors of La Sale County, and Deputy
Sheriff Brown of Marshall County.


Sheriff Slain in Fight.


Sheriff Axline was shot and killed
near Varna, ILL.,, by the bandits when
he and his men attempted to halt the
robbers in their fight from Leonore,
where they had killed Bundy and
wounded Feipp in an attempted bank
robbery.


City and county police from La Sale,
Putnam and Marshall Counties and
La Sale, Peru, Peoria and other cities
were closing in about the bandits.


The five desperados gained entrance
to the Lenore Bank during the night,
apparently through coal chute. When
Bundy, accompanied by Feipp, opened
for business shortly before 8 am, they
were confronted by the robbers, who
fled, abandoning their automobile. As
they neared a cornfield the robbers
split up, four taking to the highway
and one dashing into the field


Bundy and Fiepp followed the man
into the field and overpowered him.


Farm Boy Kidnapped.


The four who had escaped encoun-
tered a farmer and his 13-year old
son driving to Leonore. Forcing the
farmer from his car, they compelled
the boy to remain and returned toward
the city.


They came upon Bundy and Feipp
as they were marching their prisoner
from the field. The four bandits
opened fire and Bundy and Feipp re-
piled. In the exchange the two men
fell wounded, Bundy mortally and
Feipp seriously.


The freed robber Joined his COM
panions and the five sped south.


The boy hostage was later freed, un-
harmed.


One of the bank robbers committed
suicide in preference to capture.

The widow of Allen B. Wilson,

her husbands death under the
employers liability act today,

commissioner of the United States
Employees Compensation, entered

son and her three children.


Mrs. Wilson, who was repre-.

myer and Joseph A. Kaufman,

shortly after the tragedy. The
claim was opposed by the insurer,
Maryland Casualty Company, on
grounds that the laws of Mary.
land, where the tragedy occurred,
should govern the amount of the
award.


Further opposition was based
on the claim that Mr.. Wilson,
shot from ambush by unidentified
gunmen, was not injured in the
course of his employment.

full amount of the $500. the
maximum under District law, is
paid. The insurer must also pay
the funeral expenses of the route
agent. The Maryland compensa-
tion law fixes $4,000 as the maxi
mum award for death.

McCOOK, Neb., June 3 Q.N.SO.
The grim specters of hunger,
disease and thirst roved over this
stricken territory today in the wake
of the worst flood in Nebraska's
history.


AS the raging torrents subsidized
and the wind died down, survivors
and rescue workers tabulated the
casualties as follows:


Dead, 105; missing, 210; injured,
500; homeless, 5000; marooned,
1000.


Red Cross workers and Ma
tional Guardsmen were striving
against almost overwhelming odds
to give some measure of relief to
the injured, marooned and home
| less.


There was a dire need for hos
pital supplies, foodStuffS and
clothing.


Drinking Water Gone


Although water surged all about
them, survivors might as well be
in the midst of a desert, for the
water, doctors warned, was reek-
ing with disease germs.


The rescue work was carried on
in Skiffs, patched rowboats and
on improvised RATS. All efforts
were bent toward saving those
still alive and bodies spotting the
CHASTITY waste were passed by for
the time.


The flooded zone extends for
200 miles along the swollen basin
of the Republican River. Property
damage has been conservatively
estimated at $12,000,000.


The Republican Valley was the
first hit by the disaster. Next a
tornado leveled the farms and
small homes near York. Close On
it's heels the South Platte River
climbed it's banks and inundated
the countryside. The Nemaha
River was the next to overflow
only minutes before cloudburst
struck Louisville.


The Rev. Thomas Bragg and
his wife were trapped in their
home at Cambridge.


Wait Death Together


Arms wrapped round each
other they waited bravely as the
muddy brown tide swirled higher
and higher. For hours they clung
together. At last the pastor
gasped:


II can't stand it any longer"


With his last bit Of strength
he pushed his wife back on their
small porch and slid beneath the
murky waves. His body was
later recovered.


Mrs. Truman c. Mosely climbed
to the highest tree with her
daughter, Jean, S, when the
flood hit their home south of
Cambridge. There they clung all
Friday night until they were
sighted by an airplane Saturday
morning and later rescued.


But in the meantime, her hus-
band had struck off for another
haven with their 20-months-old
son, Kenneth. He swan toward
ridge, but was sucked under.
A current carried him to safety
but the baby periShed.

in an attempt to carry food

Nemaha River overflowed at Falls

of rich farmland.

bodies of those drowned in the
southwestern Nebraska flood area

ment before the British House OF

AUBURNDALE, Mass, March 80
R.-Conmodity prices about-faced
during the closing week Of the month,
registering a substantial increase.
Three major groups paved the way for
a higher price average, namely, in
dustrial and agricultural products
and also livestock. European war
scares, coupled with less favorable
agricultural growing conditions en-
couraged greater speculative activity.
A check-up shows that out of IA indi-
vidual groups, eight advanced, three
remained unchanged, while three
groups continued the downward price
movement which was characteristic of


Industrial prices moved upward fol-
lowing eight consecutive weekly de-
clines. Strength is attributable to
higher quotations for leather, nom
ferrous metals and textiles. Prelimin-
ary figures covering industrial activity
indicate only a limited seasonal con-
traction for the month of March.


Farm Prices Strongest.


Agricultural prices recorded greatest
strength of any one group, which was
due to the psychological effect Of the
dust storm which is heralded as q
forerunner of drouth, crop deteriora-
ton, and another year of subnormal
yields. During the week prices for
wheat, corn, oats, cotton. eggs, sugar,
f1axseed. and butter averaged higher
than the previous week. Declines
were noted in the case of wool and
rye.


Livestock prices regained part of
the reaction recorded a week ago.
The index failed to approach the high
point in the second week of March,
but higher prices for cattle and hogs
more than counteracted weakness in
sheep and lambs, and established the
price level well above last weeks
figure.


Non-ferrous metals recorded a size
able gain under the leadership of
higher prices for lead, silver and tin.

clined were ferrous metals, which was
due to lower quotations for steel
scrap. The paper and pulp index

Though the ship subsidy bill has
moved another notch toward enact

The bill. already passed by the
House, was approved by the Senate
Commerce Committee yesterday with

Senator Murphy, Democrat. Of Iowa

to base earnings only on their own
investment in a ship, not its total
cost.

sides for the present ocean mail pay
ments. The Government could pay
the difference between American and
foreign costs of ship construction,
provided the difference did not exceed
40 per cent Of the cost. 1t also could
pay a subsidy to make up the differ
ence between costs of American and
foreign crews.


Shipowners could borrow from the
Reconstruction Finance Corp. three
quarters of the money they might
need for their share of the cost of
constructing new ships.

Fleet "Pepco" Barry singled

lor fumbled the ball. Bozek made

grunted along. All this and much besides -
the old sense of wonder as to how and why
and whence - came back, but rather sur
prisingly Ma and Da did not, and the people
of Malu were sad and silent, as if the Sailo
wasn't fun, as it used to be.


They just waited, looking out at the Sailo
which had stopped and sat on the water,
bobbing little, just as the white gulls sat.
The pig noise had ceased, leaving the day very
quiet. A canoe, not like those of Malu, left
beach with long paddles scrapng into the
fiat water The grown-ups spoke together
They were angry, and grunted bad words
like the pig had the time it ate up its babies.


When the canoe came closer, he saw that
white man and a white woman sat in her and
we're padded by two brown men. For space,

CHINA was originally chinaware,


signitying literally ware from
China. This was pottery and earth
enware Of fine, almost transparent
texture, manufactured Of course in
China, and introduced into Europe
in the sixteenth century, through Por-
tugal.


For two centuries thereafter, prac-
tically all the chinawart so-called
came from the Orient. from China
particularly. Early in the eighteenth
century. however, Europe began set
ting up its own manufactures. Some
Of these became famous. The first
factory. for instance, was built In
Dresden. which became known
throughout the continent for its ex-
cellent product.


The Persian name for earthenware
of this type is chini, which was the
name by which it was described
throughout India and the East gen.
orally.


The close trade relationship between
England and India. coupled with the
natural tendency to cut down a longer
term for a commodity commonly used,
resulted in shortening chinaware to
china. This became the generic Name
regardless Of origin-of the utensils
with which We are familiar.

FORT WORTH, Tex, November

death and six others were injured in
a fire which destroyed the Hollings-
worth Apartments here today.


The dead were not Immediately
identified. Most of the injured were
hurt in leaping from second-story
windows to escape the flames.


The fire started at tbs am.


An explosion was reported to have
preceded the fire.


The injured included:


Mrs. Minnie Robinson, 49, fractured
skull.


Miss Essie Martin, 81, sprained
ankles.


Mrs. Jesse Bowden, broken leg.


Mrs. Myrtle Daugherty, operator Of
the apartment, was awakened by the
screams of FIRE" She could not To-
cate the blaze Immediately. but ran
out Of a rears door.


Mr.. and Mrs Ray Mason, asleep
downstairs, were awakened by the
blast and fed from the house in their
night attire.


Firemen said they believed the fire
originated in the room Of Mrs. Cary
Cashion and Mrs. Bell Stevens. They
were unable to account for the blast.


The building is owned by Mrs. j.
M. Hollingsworth.


Mrs. Bowden leaped from second
floor window, clutched back yard
fence paling and screamed for help.
Mr.. and Mrs. Herbert Voss, operators
of next door apartment house, heard
her cries and found her grasping the
paling, one Of her legs broken.


Shocked and terrified. Mrs. Bowden
clung to the paling. The couple was
forced to tear down the fence and
carry woman and fence away from
the flames and into the street.

RIO DE JANEIRO, November 28.-
Some political sources said today the
uprising in northeast Brazil and in
the capital itself, which the govern
ment crushed with loyal troops, was
but the first sharp conflict between
Socialistic and Fascist trends.


With the dual rebellions by seditious
troops in the federal district crushed
and the last of the northeastern in
surgents put to fight. government
authorities said the entire nation ap-
parently was under control.


Twelve rebels were known dead and
five of the loyal army forces wounded
after the governments artillery and
aviation smashed the abortive revolts
Yesterday at the aviation school in the
federal district and the Sd Infantry
barracks at Praia Vermelha, on the
beach beneath Sugar Loaf Mountain.


800 Held Prisoners.


The government announced 1t held
800 participants in the local uprisings
prisoners and word came from the
State of iRo Grande Do Notre, scene
of the earlier northeastern revolt, that
Gov. Raphael Fernandes resumed his
post.


The Governor notified President
Getulio Vargas, "the rebels abandoned
Natal after a great amount OF sack
ing. Means have been taken to nor
malize completely Natal and its COM
mlmications."


Planes and ships pressed a search
for steamship Santos on which the
northeast rebels were reported to have
fed Natal, and authorities took pre-
cautions under the State of seige to
maintain control. One authority,
however, said:


"Brazil's real political struggle is
between Fascism and Socialism"


First Socialist Efforts Seen.


This politician, who asked that his
name be withheld, said the abortive
uprisings Sunday in Pernambuco and
Rio Grande do Norte and yesterday in
Rio de Janeiro we're only the first
effort by the socialistic National Lib
Grating Alliance to create subverslve
outbreaks bidding for national power.
4 THE alliance, which opposes Fas-
eist trend, sees within Fascism two
main currents" this source said.
y "One is inside the government itself,
hoping for establishment OF military
dictatorship.


j. THE other Is the more theatrical
integralism, which serves the ends OF
those of Fascist thought within the
government and the military, and /:
therefore tolerated by the same admin
lstration which in July banned the
alliance throughout Brazil.


= "Brazil's army (65,00O conscrlpts
and 5000 officers) is apparently torn
between Fascist and socialistic strains.


Prestes' Name Recurs.


MANY commissioned officers
and privates incline toward socialism,
whereas the higher command is in
clined toward Fascist theology.


The rising in Pernambuco, Rio
Grande do Notre and Rio de Janeiro
was the first subversive movement in
a series rumored to be destined to
embrace all Brazil from December 18
under the leadership of Luiz Carlos
Prestes, chieftain of organized Social
ism in Brazil"


The National Liberating Alliance
itself circulated manifesto through
out the nation denying charges by the
government that the organization was
communistic.


The manifesto said the alliances
aims we're to appropriate foreign cap
italistic enterprises. respect Brazilian
national enterprises, break up the
"feudal" system Of large land hold
ings and give more land to small

NEW YORK, October 12-Wall
Street turned bullish again this week,
after more than three weeks of fret
ting over the threat of war and the
course of business.


Industrial shares came back to
around their recovery peaks of mid
September. and rails regained, roughly,
half of their losses.


The subsistence Ct the war fright
was most notable in the bond market.
where foreign issues scored their best
gains in long time. although Italians
slid off somewhat at the end of the
week


Wall Street still found the news
from Europe confusing, but houses
with London connections were encour-
aged by the more hopeful tenor of
advices from that center and the re-
covery in the London Stock Exchange.


Expect Favorable Trend.


Furthermore. with the automobile
industry smoothing out the problems
of new model production and plan
ming to resume production at full tilt
by November, financial circles were led
to look for increasingly favorable busi-
ness statistics during coming weeks.


The September business showing
had been little spotty. what with the
automobile industry almost shut down
in preparation for its earlier than
usual 1886 presentations, the btu
minous coal strike causing momen-
tary slump in freight movement, and
retail trade hampered early in the
month by adverse weather


AS result, statistical indices of
business activity had wavered, and
while underlying sentiment in Wall
Street remained optimistic, an inclina-
ton to wait and see was natural.


Kindled BY Warning.


Bullish flames in the share market
appeared to have been kindled by the
warning issued in a public address
Wednesday evening by President Gay
Of the Stock Exchange that danger
GUS inflationary boom might develop,
leading to another crash like 1929, if
the Federal Reserve and the Treasury
do not apply the brakes.


But this seemed to be only the
kindling spark, although on Thursday
the stock market experienced its
widest advance, measured by price
averages, since last June.


Commodity prices continued their
advance during the early days of the
week, boosting the Associated Press
daily index of 20 basic staples to new
recovery highs. But the movement
leveled of later, with wheat and cot
ton slipping back a little. Rubber.
copper, silk. hides and a few other
staples scored net gains for the week,
however.

NEW YORK, July 13.-Tourists who
visit Turkey this Summer will see
q most democratic assembly of ecclesi-
astical dress, according to the educa-
ton department Of the American Ex-
press Co. The law forbidding ecclesi-
astics in Turkey to wear clerical dress,
except at religious ceremonies, came
into force this month.


When the law was first promulgated
six months ago, many of the clerics,
particularly the Armenians, at once
set about acquiring lay clothes and
have now been wearing them for some
time. The majority, however. waited
until this month and the Greek priests
have only recently had their long hair
cut. They will be seen on the street
dressed alike in double-breasted suits,
ties and Homburg hats, all of black.
Lama priests have abandoned their
flowing garments and have taken on
an English haberdashery. Moslem
priests have trimmed their boards and
adopted uniform dress and may be
seen wearing lounge suits of varying
colors and anything from cap to a
bowler hat as headgear.

Secretary Dern and Gen. Malin Craig

Deep regret at the death Of Lieut..
Gen. Hunter Liggett was expressed
yesterday by Secretary Dern and Gen.
Malin Craig, Army chief of staff.


Dern said:


II am greatly distressed to learn
of the death of Gen. Liggett: His
career exemplifies the finest in Amer
ican leadership. His professional
skill, his genius for command, COM
bined with his warm. human sympa-
thy, his eager concern for the welfare
of his men, had won for him a rank
with the great military leaders Of all
times. In his death the Army has
lost one of its greatest characters and
the country one Of its ablest serv-
ants"


Gen. Craig said:


Gen Liggett was real leader. He
commanded not only the respect and
esteem OF all of the men under him,
but also their genuine affection. With
the exception of Gen. Pershing, Gen.
Liggett did more to bring about our
victory in the World War than any
other American officer"

map of the Pacific Oceans floor.
where towering undersea mountains
and huge abysses make land topog-
raphy seem puny, was displayed here
today. 1t Is the work Of Capt. Claude
Banks Mayo, attached to the thir-
teenth naval district.


The map was designed out OF q big
plank and thousands Of bronze nails
through use Of sounding records.


Capt. Mayos articles on the Pacinc
ocean floor have attracted worldwide
interest among photographers. Many
have studied his map. the first ever
made Of the sub-continent between
America and Asia.


The veteran naval ofiicer started the
novel work while captain Of the Navy
tanker U. 8. Rsmapo. transporting
cargoes Of fuel oil.


He became interested In the Sonic
sounding device, which tested the
depth of water every half hour. He
started experiments that produced his
strange map.


The ships of,cers became inter-
ested and helped.

I'VE took the plank and drove
bronze nails, made especially, into It
at spots corresponding to the places
where we made the soundings," Capt.
Mayo said.


"One inch on the nail was equal to
5000 fathoms. II the sounding
showed 1000 fathoms we'd drive the
nail In two inches. Seventeen thou
sand three hundred and sixty-nine
soundines were taken to finish the re-
lief map"


The map, completed with a mixture
of asbestos, water and glue, showed
huge mountain ranges, q few Of whose
peaks protrude above the water to
form the Hawaiian Islands, Wake
Island, Midway Island and Guam.


In the area between Guam and the
Philippines, which Capt. Mayo calls
the bad lands" the map showed six
mile-deep gulches.

erybody Of the peril aboard.


Jack" being the nautical term for
flag. the Yellow Jack became the
recognized and Official quarantine
pennant, as well as the synonym. for
yellow fever flag; while Yellow Jack
became the slang. synonymous phrase
for yellow fever.

A behind-the-scenes fight to a
finish by the combined revenue
enforcement armies Of the Treas
ury has licked the "alky" snug
gler and alien liquor runner,
Treasury reports showed today.


While Treasury officials from
Secretary Mongenthau down
through the ranks of enforcement
agencies were chary of flat claims
of victory, they pointed to one
index, liquor withdrawal pay
ments, and another, the absence
of rum ships lowering outside the
danger zone.


Increases Noted


Payments on legal Withdrawals
in June, 1894, were 100000.
Payments for June this year were
$13, 200, 900, in round figures. The
same figures were reported for
May Of this year, over last May;
April of this year showed double
the withdrawal payments over last
year. Proportionate gains were
recorded for February and March
over the preceding year.


Treasury officials pointed out
that low withdrawal payments
were strong indication that the
supply was being met by outside
sources, presumably smuggled
liquor or alcohol for bootleg man
ufacture. Similarly, high with
drawal figures show that the IL
legal supply is failing.


The Surest sign of victory, they
claim. is the absence of rum ships.
Some months ago, President
Roosevelt attracted nationwide
attention to the menace of boot
legged alcohol, most of it from
foreign sources.


There were more than 10 rum
running vessels lowering outside
the legal danger zone, laden
mostly with alcohol. The Treas
ury today reported only four are
left. These are all on the Atlantic
coast, and are under constant
guard. Their exact location is not
being advertised, but enforcement
officers know where they are
anchored. .-..


Treaties On Horizon /


Drying up this outlaw alcohol
and liquor was done through the
combined efforts of six enforce
ment groups in the Treasury, in
cooperation with other depart
ment Sleuths and those of Can
ada.


Every week these six groups
have held a Crime conference"
in the Treasury Building, to pool
their efforts for the next weeks
operations. When the liquor fugi-
tives, on ship or shore, attempted
to cross to Canada, agents of that
country took up at the border
line, armed with information
from American sources.


Canada is now reported trou-
bled by the same danger from
smugglers. Under the new anti
smuggling act, the United States
is preparing to negotiate treaties,
notably with Great Britain, Swe-
den and France, designed to
tighten the fence even more.

The Hauptmann jury rejoiced today
in two new-found diversions-parlor
games and bus rides.


Time has been hanging heavily on
the hands of the housewives and farm
ers, the carpenter and former semi
pro base ball player, all accustomed
to hard work. Their main diversion
is walking.


During the week end recess. how
ever. they had a party in their Union
Hotel rooms. playing parlor games
and guessing riddles. They went, too,
for a ride in a school bus through
nearby towns.


Philip Hockenbury, Clinton Town
ship laborer caught slight cold over
the week end and had his Sunday
breakfast and a steak dinner sent to
his room.


Jury Has Sweet Tooth.


The other jurors dined behind
screens in the hotel dining room on
fruit cup. cream of chicken soup,
turkey with dressing. waffles with
sirup, lettuce salad with Russian
dressing, cranberry sauce, celery,
olives. radishes. hot biscuits and
"sunnysilver pie" with ice cream and
coffee.


The Hauptmann jury has a sweet
tooth, and "sunnysilver pie" is its ia
vorite dessert. This pie. specially of
the hotel. has a f1aky crust, a creamy
filling with a trace of lemon and a
whipped cream top with a little pat
tern made by the point of Knife.


The jury also likes ice cream. Since
the trial opened only one juror has
refused dessert-that was Howard v.
Biggs, former bookkeeper of Clinton
Township, and he did it only once.


The jurors have hearty appetites
and like the hotel food-in fact, Mrs.
Rosie Pill and Mrs. Verna Snyder,
who sit together at the long table.
say they are gaining weight. Both
women now weigh about $50 pounds.


Life Of the Party.


Mrs. Snyder does not eat butter
and. passes hers over to Mrs. Ethel
Stockton, who sits next to the jury
foreman, Charles Walton, sr., at din
ner. Mrs. Stockton. the youngest
woman on the jury. is really the life
of the party.


Jury Constable Oden Bangstrom
sits at the head of the table, which
looks like family reunion party. At
the foot is another constable, Mrs.
Pearl Conover, who is almost as large
as Mrs. Pill.


Because the hotel dining room
crowd stared. the screens covered
with flower -sprigged wallpaper were
set up to shield the Jurors. But other
diners see them filing in and often
hear the party laugh.

The Franklin Delano Roosevelts
quietly observed the eve of their 30th
wedding anniversary last night, but
preparations for a family reunion
today showed many little signs OF
sentiment and remembrance.


Because of the illness of Louis
Howe. chief Of the Presidents secre-
tariat, the only entry thus far on the
Sunday schedule was family dinner
and on that dinners menu was
scrambled eggs.


Almost invariably during these Sc
years. the RooseveltS have served
scrambled eggs Sunday night and
that custom goes back to the wedding
day. Among the gifts was a hand
some silver chafing dish. Mrs. Roose-
welt presided over it at their flrst

terfered.

lege seemed unlikely to materlallze.

ization" for her.

locket, with initials intertwned,

ROCKVILLE. Md, August 22.-Two
Baltimore & Ohio passenger trains
an eastbound express and west
bound local-marked time for more
than 20 minutes just before dark here
last night while members Of the local
Volunteer Fire Department removed
q horse from trestle.


The chestnut mount. property of
colored man who lives short distance
east Of the Rockville station, wandered
from his pasture onto the nearby
trestle and found ie-walking too
complicated for four legs. One leg
slipped through an opening and then
another.


The engineer Of the local saw the
animal and stopped his train before
reaching the trestle. Spectators and
members of the train crew ran up
the track and tagged the speeding
express. Others phoned the Fire De-
partment.


Under the direction of Clarence e.
Anders, chief engineer of the depart
ment, the horse was roped. fore and
aft, lifted and laid on his side. His
legs were then hobbled and by means
of sliding planks he was hauled across
the ties.


Unbound, the horse struggled to his
feet and walked away with no more
than q slight limp.
